eea_parameters.name: Affective grooming/touch from trusted others (adult social touch)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Beyond infancy, ancestral adults maintained social bonds through frequent affiliative body contact: the human homolog of primate grooming. Primate grooming is fundamentally about the intimacy of massage, where skin stimulation triggers endorphin release and underwrites social bonding. Ancestral adults lived in high-touch social fields where reassuring, stress-buffering touch from trusted others (partners, kin, allies) was a routine, ever-present channel of social and physiological regulation.

eea_value.mechanism: skin stimulation -> endorphin release (bonding) and vagal/cortisol regulation (stress buffering)
eea_value.reciprocity: bidirectional: giver and receiver both benefit physiologically
eea_value.adult_social_touch: frequent affiliative body contact / grooming-homolog from trusted others

eea_parameters.modern_default: Adult-to-adult affiliative touch is sharply curtailed in WEIRD societies by personal-space norms, professionalization of touch, and screen-mediated relationships; trusted-other touch is increasingly confined to a single partner or absent entirely, and remote communication carries none of it.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Loss of routine affiliative touch from trusted others removes a bonding and stress-buffering input that operated continuously in ancestral social life. Partner/trusted-other touch buffers acute stress more effectively than verbal support alone, and the benefit is bidirectional. This channel is physical-contact-only and cannot be delivered by remote or volumetric technology.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable supply of affiliative touch from trusted others (the grooming homolog), present as an ongoing relational channel; not one-off or transactional touch, and not mere co-presence without contact.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): argued, not yet tested. No forager measurement of adult social-touch frequency exists; the ancestral claim is inferred from primate grooming, and the modern stress-buffering studies test the mechanism, not this ancestral value. The one human scan study of a partner's touch was read by its authors as less opioid release, which they call unexpected (ext 2281); such a scan cannot separate release from a change in receptors (ext 2280). In six small-scale societies, grooming one another took about 0.8 percent of the day, against the 4 percent a model of 69 primate species predicts for humans, while time in conversation was as predicted (ext 3607).

The physical stimulation of the skin triggers the release of endorphins in the brain.
evidence.content: Primate grooming is not about removing fleas - it is about the intimacy of massage. Physical stimulation of the skin triggers endorphin release in the brain. Low-level pain associated with generalized stresses is dealt with by the endorphin system, creating a sense of wellbeing a

Most sociologists would agree that societies like those in the Mediterranean countries (e.g., Spain, France, Italy, Greece, Turkey, Egypt) are contact societies, whereas the more northern societies in countries such as Holland, Great Britain, and the United States are not.

eea_parameters.name: Falling evening ambient temperature as a second sleep-onset cue
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Outside thermally buffered shelter, ancestral evenings carried a reliable nocturnal drop in ambient temperature that paralleled dusk. This descending thermal ramp coincides with the endogenous evening fall in core body temperature that gates sleep onset, plausibly acting as a second zeitgeber-like onset cue alongside light. The baseline environment thus paired a dimming light gradient with a falling temperature gradient at the day-night transition.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Climate-controlled indoor environments hold ambient temperature roughly constant across the 24-hour cycle, removing the evening cooling ramp; evening heat (and sometimes overheated bedrooms) can also oppose the core-temperature fall required for sleep onset.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: By flattening the daily thermal cycle, modern housing removes a candidate onset cue that historically co-occurred with dusk and reinforced circadian timing, potentially leaving light as the sole (and now corrupted) entrainment channel.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Direction and timing of the evening ambient-temperature change (a falling ramp at dusk), not absolute thermostat setpoint or daytime comfort.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested once. Yetish et al. 2015 found sleep fell during the nightly drop in ambient temperature in Hadza, San and Tsimane; one research group, association only. That temperature acts as a sleep cue is argued.

evidence.author_quote: The sleep period consistently occurred during the nighttime period of falling environmental temperature, was not interrupted by extended periods of waking, and terminated, with vasoconstriction, near the nadir of daily ambient temperature
evidence.content: In three pre-industrial groups (Hadza, San and Tsimane), people slept about 6 to 7 hours a night, did not sleep longer than industrial adults, and fell asleep as the night got cooler.

eea_parameters.name: Sleep timing/phase alignment to the biological night (not a fixed duration target)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestrally, sleep occurred within a stable phase relationship to the solar/circadian night: onset about three hours after sunset (3.3 hours on average among Hadza, San and Tsimane, ext 2224; about three hours in rural Haiti without electricity, ext 3903), offset near or before dawn, with the sleep episode anchored to internal circadian time. Field data from three preindustrial societies (Hadza, San, Tsimane) place habitual sleep within a window in the rough range of ~6-7 hours of nocturnal sleep; subsistence horticulturalists on Tanna, Vanuatu, slept about 7.4 to 7.9 hours (ext 2813). The ancestral feature that counts is the alignment of the sleep episode to circadian phase; the hour count differed between groups. Total nightly sleep duration in such groups is modest and overlaps the lower end of modern recommendations; there is no evidence of a hard-wired 8-9 hour requirement.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Industrial schedules set wake (and increasingly sleep) times by clock and alarm rather than by internal time, producing chronic 'social jetlag' - a standing offset between the endogenous circadian phase and the socially imposed sleep window. In a large Central-European dataset ~69% experience >=1 hour of social jetlag and about one-third >=2 hours; ~80% of workers wake by alarm; population chronotype has drifted later while workday sleep has shortened.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is primarily one of phase, not amount. Even when total sleep is adequate, misalignment between biological and social clocks is associated with metabolic harm (e.g. social jetlag raises overweight odds and predicts BMI in the overweight, with an effect more than half that of sleep duration, after controlling for duration itself). Across 43 studies of 231,648 people, social jetlag went with higher body mass index and 1.2 times the odds of overweight (Arab et al. 2024), and in the high-quality studies of a review of 68 with higher body mass index, waist, systolic blood pressure and HbA1c (Bouman et al. 2023). In 60,977 UK adults, regular sleep and wake times predicted lower mortality more strongly than sleep duration did (Windred et al. 2024). Chasing a duration number while ignoring phase misses the operative variable.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Sleep timing/phase - the alignment of the sleep episode to internal circadian night - NOT sleep duration.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Night-anchored sleep of about 5.7 to 7.1 hours is measured by actigraphy in three forager societies (Yetish et al. 2015), in 33 Hadza adults across 393 days of recording in all (6.25 hours a night, with stronger circadian rhythms than Western populations; Samson et al. 2017) and in Toba/Qom (de la Iglesia et al. 2015); camping studies move phase while duration holds. Actigraphy only, and parts of the interpretation are disputed. The two camping experiments (Wright et al. 2013, ext 610; Stothard et al. 2017, ext 613) come from the same laboratory and share authors.

evidence.author_quote: Here we show that electrical lighting and the constructed environment is associated with reduced exposure to sunlight during the day, increased light exposure after sunset, and a delayed timing of the circadian clock as compared to a summer natural 14h40min:9h20min light-dark cycle camping. Furthermore, we find that after exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time such that the beginning of the internal biological night occurs at sunset and the end of the internal biological night occurs before wake time just after sunrise.
evidence.content: After exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time: biological night begins at sunset and ends just after sunrise; electrical lighting is associated with a delayed clock.

evidence.author_quote: Following the week of exposure to natural lighting, all measured markers of internal circadian time were ~2h earlier (Fig 3., all p<0.01; Bonferroni correction required p<0.0167, one tailed) and remarkably, melatonin onset occurred on average near sunset, the melatonin midpoint occurred in the middle of the solar night, and melatonin offset occurred before wake time just after sunrise. Sleep timing was related to circadian timing after electrical lighting-constructed conditions and less so after exposure to only natural light (Supplemental information Table S1 and Fig. S2). The advance in timing of melatonin onset was significantly larger than changes in sleep start and wake times which changed by ~1.2h (Fig. 3, both p<0.02; Bonferroni correction required p<0.025, two tailed). Weekly sleep duration (6.7±0.9h electrical versus 6.8h±0.7h natural lighting; p=0.268, twotailed) and sleep efficiency (87.6±5.6% electrical versus 87.0±4.6% natural lighting; p=0.49, two-tailed) did not significantly change indicating that a change in sleep amount or efficiency did not contribute to the current findings.
evidence.content: One week of natural light advanced all circadian markers ~2h (melatonin onset near sunset) while sleep duration and efficiency were statistically unchanged: the change was in circadian PHASE/timing, not sleep amount.

evidence.author_quote: We have previously shown that exposure to a natural summer 14 hr 40 min:9 hr 20 min light-dark cycle entrains the human circadian clock to solar time, such that the internal biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise [1]. Here we show the beginning of the biological night and sleep occur earlier after a week exposure to a natural winter 9 hr 20 min:14 hr 40 min light-dark cycle as compared to the modern electrical lighting environment.
evidence.content: Replicates and extends Wright 2013: natural light entrains the clock so the biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise; under a natural WINTER light-dark cycle the biological night and sleep occur earlier than under modern electrical lighting.

evidence.author_quote: After exposure to the natural light-dark cycle while weekend camping, melatonin onset and midpoint were ~1.4 hr and ~1.0 hr earlier within the same participants compared to the weekday (p<0.01; with large and medium effect sizes for condition [η2G = 0.45 and 0.20, respectively]), despite no change in sleep timing.
evidence.content: A single weekend of natural-light camping advanced melatonin onset/midpoint ~1.4h/~1.0h within the same participants DESPITE no change in sleep timing: circadian phase, not sleep amount, is the variable that moves.

eea_parameters.name: What standing buys (children)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Across 33 non-industrial societies, higher-status men had more children (meta-analysis of 288 results, overall r 0.19). The effect in foragers (Zr 0.18) was about the same as in farmers and herders. Status worked mostly through more mates and more births, less through fewer child deaths, and the effect on surviving children was about a third smaller where marriage was monogamous. Better hunters had more surviving children in five societies (Ache, Hadza, !Kung, Lamalera, Meriam). Among the Tsimane both dominance and prestige went with higher fertility, prestige most.
eea_parameters.modern_default: In industrial societies the link between men's status and number of children is weaker than in pre-industrial societies, and the sexes differ: men with higher incomes still have more children, mainly because poor men more often stay childless, while higher income in women and more education in both sexes typically go with fewer children (ext 5072). Professional status-seeking takes the time and money that children need.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Status-seeking was tied to children; the motive still runs while the payoff in children has weakened or reversed. Across industrial populations, wealth, measured as income, went with higher fertility in 8 of 12 longitudinal findings, and income went with more children in men and fewer in women (Stulp and Barrett 2016); in three industrial samples the link between men's wealth and their number of children was the weakest of eleven human samples, though still positive (ext 3657), and in Britain higher-income men had more children only because low-income men were more often childless, while women's own income went with fewer children (ext 3658).
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for the ancestral link, men only. Strongest study: von Rueden and Jaeggi 2016 (ext 731), 288 effects from 33 societies; weakness: very different status measures pooled, all correlational. Among the Batek, 45 years of data showed no link between foraging success or sharing and lifetime reproductive success (Kraft et al. 2019, ext 1583); with 44 adults, where the authors calculate that about 200 are needed to detect the average forager effect (ext 1584), the study was too small to test it. Two studies measured raiding: among the Waorani, men who raided more often than average did not have more wives or children (ext 897); among the Nyangatom, younger men's raiding showed no link to wives or children, while elders whom peers named as prolific raiders had more of both (ext 892). The modern link is tested: in industrial populations wealth, measured as income, went with higher fertility in 8 of 12 longitudinal findings, men's income went with more children and women's income and education with fewer (Stulp and Barrett 2016); the grade of this row covers the ancestral link only. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 770, 897.

eea_parameters.name: Effort-to-outcome contingency (closed-loop, self-attributable)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Subsistence effort sat in a short, visible, self-attributable causal loop: the same individual who tracked, dug, gathered, knapped, or built directly observed the outcome of that effort, on a timescale of minutes to days. Effort-outcome links were embodied and legible - you could see whether your action produced the result. The evolved controllability circuitry (vmPFC detects response-outcome contingency and, when contingency is present, inhibits the dorsal-raphe passivity default) was calibrated to environments where such contingency was routinely present and detectable, and where experiences of control immunized against later helplessness.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Much modern productive effort is decoupled from any visible, self-attributable outcome: work is mediated by long opaque chains, algorithmic management, and electronic monitoring that reduce decision latitude; rewards are detached in time and attribution from the effort that earned them; and many roles offer high demand with low control. The closed loop between one's own action and an observable result is frequently broken.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Because passivity is the unlearned default that only switches OFF when controllability is detected, environments that obscure the effort-outcome link don't feel neutral - they default the organism toward helplessness-type physiology. The gap is the loss of routinely detectable, self-attributable contingency, which population health data link to elevated disease risk (low job control predicts coronary disease independent of grade).
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Reliably PRESENT and DETECTABLE response-outcome contingency that the actor can attribute to their own effort - not mere busyness, throughput, or nominal 'autonomy.' What must be restored is the closed, legible loop between action and observed result, not the quantity of work.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): argued, not yet tested. No study measures how visible the link between effort and outcome was in forager work; the ancestral claim is a mismatch synthesis (van Vugt et al. 2024). The Whitehall II and rodent controllability findings test the modern side and the mechanism, not this ancestral value.

eea_parameters.name: Task diversity within the subsistence day
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: A forager's day cycled through a wide and shifting portfolio of tasks - tracking, gathering, digging, processing, toolmaking/repair, child-tending, food sharing, travel - recruiting varied skills and continually engaging the appetitive SEEKING/exploration system across novel and changing problems. The evolved exploratory-pursuit substrate (mesolimbic-dopamine SEEKING) is built for persistent inquisitive engagement with a varied environment, not for indefinitely repeating one narrow operation.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Industrial and much digital work narrows the day to repetitive, specialized, often single-task operation - high repetition, low task variety, minimal novel problem-solving - with the SEEKING system left chronically under-stimulated by the work itself and frequently redirected onto engineered supernormal substitutes (feeds, games, variable-ratio rewards) off the clock.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The gap is the collapse from a high-variety, skill-diverse subsistence portfolio to narrow repetitive specialization, under-engaging the exploratory-pursuit system whose canonical evolved function is varied engagement with a changing world. No study in Cor measures forager task diversity.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Genuine variety of self-directed, skill-recruiting tasks across the day that engage exploration and problem-solving - not nominal 'multitasking' (rapid switching among equally shallow operations) and not enrichment proxies bolted on outside the core work.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade: argued, not yet tested. Van Vugt et al. 2024 describe ancestral work as small-group, embodied, skill-based and autonomy-rich (ext 583). They do not measure task diversity. The substrate is Panksepp's SEEKING system (ext 251, 397). No study in Cor links task variety itself to health or mood.

eea_parameters.name: Acquisition effort (calories are physically worked for)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Food had to be physically acquired: walked to, foraged, dug, hunted, and processed. Among the Hadza, GPS-measured daily walking distances average about 11.4 km for men and 5.8 km for women (Pontzer et al. 2012, 30 adults over 11 days) and, in a larger sample of 179 people over 2,078 person-days, 12.9 km for men and 7.6 km for women (Wood et al. 2021, ext 3418), and women also spend several hours digging; broader hunter-gatherer daily travel is on the order of ~10 km. This embeds substantial obligate movement and a real energetic and time cost between hunger and calories. Note: the absolute activity premium over sedentary moderns is modest (hunter-gatherer PAL ~1.8-1.9 vs ~1.6 for desk workers, ~15% higher), so the baseline is 'embedded all-day effort,' not extreme athleticism.

eea_value.note: Distances are GPS means for the Hadza (Pontzer et al. 2012). They are not work hours; for work hours see EEA-SUBS-04.
eea_value.hadza_distance_source: Pontzer et al. 2012, PLoS ONE, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0040503 (GPS, means; SD 2.1 men, 1.7 women); women also dig several hours (ext 196)

eea_parameters.modern_default: Calories require essentially zero acquisition effort: hyperpalatable, energy-dense food is available on demand, pre-processed, often delivered, with no movement, foraging, or processing cost between impulse and ingestion. The effort gate that historically bounded intake is gone.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Removing the work between hunger and food eliminates a natural brake on consumption and decouples eating from the obligate daily movement it was bundled with - calories are now frictionless to obtain and detached from the physical activity that ancestrally accompanied acquisition.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Incidental, embedded, all-day acquisition movement (walking, foraging, carrying, digging) - NOT 'exercise' as a discrete bout. The mismatch is the loss of effort woven through daily food-getting, not a missing gym session. Work hours: see EEA-SUBS-04.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Hadza daily distances are GPS-measured (Pontzer et al. 2012) and forager activity levels are compared across populations (Pontzer, Wood and Raichlen 2018); the distance figures are Hadza only.

evidence.author_quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.

evidence.author_quote: Although there is much variation, PALs of hunter-gatherers average 1.9 for men and 1.8 for women, slightly below PAL scores for subsistence farmers, which average 2.1 for men and 1.9 for women. To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). In other words, typical hunter-gatherers are about as physically active as Americans or Europeans who include about an hour of exercise in their daily routine. In case you are wondering, most mammals in the wild have PALs of 3.3 or more, nearly twice as high as hunter-gatherers. Thus, comparatively speaking, humans who must hunt and gather all the food they eat and make everything they own by hand are substantially less active than average free-ranging mammals.
evidence.content: Physical Activity Level (PAL) data across populations reveals the surprising result that typical hunter-gatherers are only about 15% more active than industrialized people with desk jobs - equivalent to adding about an hour of exercise per day to a sedentary Westerner's routine.

evidence.content: In a cross-cultural sample, foragers had famine less often than farmers and herders, after controlling for habitat quality.

eea_parameters.name: Signal provenance and accountability (information from known, reputation-bearing, face-to-face sources)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestrally, virtually all socially consequential information reached an individual through known, identifiable, reputation-bearing senders within a face-to-face band. A claim about who did what, where the game was, who could be trusted, or what was dangerous arrived attached to a specific person whose track record was known and who was themselves accountable to the same dense web of relationships. There was no anonymous, unaccountable, or de-contextualized information channel: the source of a signal and the receiver's ability to weigh that source by its history were inseparable. Boehm's ethnography of forager gossip describes a band that effectively keeps a running 'dossier' on every individual - provenance was the substrate of trust.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Most information now arrives through anonymous, algorithmically-mediated, or institutionally-impersonal channels in which the sender's identity, track record, and accountability to the receiver are absent or unverifiable. The shift Tomasello describes - from face-to-face 'I-you' exchange to impersonal 'we-as-group' broadcast - is taken to an extreme by mass and digital media, where signals are detached from any reputation-bearing source the receiver can sanction or even locate.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The evolved machinery for weighing information by source reputation and face-to-face accountability is deprived of the provenance cues it was calibrated to use. Receivers must evaluate high-stakes claims from sources they cannot place in any reputational web, and senders bear little reputational cost for deception - removing the gossip/ostracism feedback loop that ancestrally policed signal honesty.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Proportion of consequential information arriving from a known, reputation-bearing, accountable source the receiver can locate and sanction - NOT raw access to information or number of contacts. A person can be flooded with information yet have almost none of it carry verifiable provenance.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): argued, not yet tested. No study measures where ancestral information came from; the claim that nearly all of it came from known people is inferred from band size and gossip ethnography. No published evidence argues the other way.

The resulting group-mindedness among all members of the cultural group (including in-group strangers) was based on a new ability to construct common cultural ground via collectively known cultural conventions, norms, and institutions.

eea_parameters.name: Gossip and narrative flow as reputation and norm transmission
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: The dominant high-bandwidth information process in ancestral groups was gossip and narrative: talk about who behaved how, who is reliable or stingy, what happened, and what one ought to do. This stream did double duty - it transmitted norms, calibrated each person's reputation in the eyes of the group, and deterred free-riding because everyone knew gossip was constantly underway and anyone could become its subject. Boehm documents gossip, ridicule, and ostracism as the primary, low-cost enforcement mechanism against free-riders (bullies, the lazy, feigners, secret meat-eaters); Henrich notes that norm violations meant 'reputational damage, gossip, and a consequent loss of marriage opportunities and allies.' Information about people and norms was the central content of the ancestral information environment.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Reputation- and norm-bearing narrative now flows largely through impersonal mass and digital media to audiences who cannot reciprocally gossip about, sanction, or verify the subjects - and much of the daily information stream is impersonal content (commercial, abstract, broadcast) rather than locally-actionable talk about known persons and norms. The tight loop in which gossip simultaneously informed, judged, and deterred within a single accountable group is broken: reputational narrative is broadcast without the reciprocal accountability that made it self-policing.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The gossip/narrative channel that ancestrally fused information transmission with reputation tracking and norm enforcement is decoupled. People consume reputational narrative about strangers they cannot sanction, and the norm-deterrence function (knowing the group is watching and will talk) is weakened in anonymous or one-to-many settings - leaving the evolved appetite for reputational narrative engaged but its enforcement payload disabled.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Reputation/norm narrative circulating within a bounded group where subjects and audience are mutually known and can reciprocally sanction - NOT raw volume of social content consumed. Doomscrolling celebrity gossip is high-volume but supplies almost no actionable, reciprocal reputational signal.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Gossip, ridicule and ostracism as norm enforcement are documented across forager ethnography (Boehm 1993, 1999; Wiessner 2014; Smith et al. 2017) and gossip deters selfishness in experiments (Feinberg et al. 2012). That modern channels weaken this function is the framework's reading, untested.

eea_parameters.name: Lifetime known-individual ceiling (~1,000)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Across a foraging lifetime an individual accumulated a bounded pool of personally known others - people met face-to-face, named, placed in a kin/alliance/reputation map, and remembered. Estimates put this cumulative lifetime roster at roughly 1,000+ distinct individuals (Hill et al. 2014, Hadza/Ache), an order of magnitude above the ~150 actively-maintained network the social brain tracks concurrently. This pool was not a single contemporaneous group: it accreted over decades through camp reshuffling, regional fission-fusion, and durable cross-camp partnerships (e.g. Ju/'hoansi hxaro). Crucially it was finite, slowly-growing, and fully reputation-indexed: nearly everyone one would ever encounter was either already known or one or two reciprocal links away, and almost no one was a true anonymous stranger. The cognitive machinery for naming, tracking reputation, and gauging trust was calibrated to a lifetime ceiling on this order, with the ~150 active-network limit (Dunbar) operating as the concurrent sub-ceiling within it.

eea_value.note: Hill et al. 2014 (Ache, Hadza; ext 606, 608): a 'social universe of about a thousand individuals'; a lifetime pool 'clearly more than 1,000'. One model-based study in two populations. For the ~150 ceiling and the 5/15/50/150 layers, see EEA-SOC-01.

eea_parameters.modern_default: A networked individual is exposed to vastly more than 1,000 distinct identities - thousands of nominal "friends"/followers plus a near-unbounded daily stream of strangers (crowds, feeds, comment sections, customer interactions). Nominal contact counts routinely run into the thousands while the genuinely-tracked inner network stays pinned near the same ~150, and only ~27.6% of those nominal ties register as genuine close friends. The result is a permanent flood of identities the reputation-tracking and trust-calibration system was never built to index: most are anonymous, non-reciprocal, never re-encountered, and carry no durable reputation, so they neither enter the lifetime roster nor decay out of it normally - they simply accumulate as un-indexable noise. The pool of actually-known, reputation-bearing people is no larger than ancestrally, but it is now embedded in an environment of effectively infinite strangers.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: EEA delivered a finite, slowly-accreting lifetime roster (~1,000+) in which virtually every encountered person was known or one reciprocal link away and carried trackable reputation; modernity delivers an unbounded firehose of identities, the overwhelming majority anonymous, non-reciprocal, and reputation-less. The mismatch is not in the size of the maintainable network (still ~150) but in the ratio of known-to-unknown: a system tuned to "almost everyone you meet is someone you can place" now operates where almost everyone you meet is someone you cannot. This chronically engages strangers as ambient novelty/threat (threat-management framing) and starves the cooperation/reputation system (M11) of the direct, repeated, reciprocal observability it evolved to run on, while the cumulative roster of genuinely-known people fails to grow despite massive nominal connection.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested once. One study estimates a lifetime pool of over 1,000 people from interaction rates and life tables in Ache and Hadza (Hill et al. 2014); model-based, two populations.

evidence.author_quote: We suggest that while residential and foraging groups are often small, there is little evidence that these groups are drawn from small communities nested within small-scale societies. evidence.content: Forager residential groups vary widely in size and composition, and people moved between many groups across a regional network, so a single fixed small band is an oversimplification.

eea_parameters.name: Co-sleeping / nighttime body contact
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral infants and young children slept in body contact with the mother and others rather than alone, extending the daytime carried-contact regime through the night. Nighttime proximity meant the touch, warmth, and physiological co-regulation channels (and likely circadian entrainment cues from the caregiver) operated continuously across the 24-hour cycle, not just during waking.
eea_parameters.modern_default: WEIRD norms favor solitary infant sleep in a separate crib or room, removing nighttime body contact for most of the sleep period; adult sleep is also frequently solitary or contact-minimized.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Solitary infant and child sleep removes the nighttime half of the ancestral continuous-contact regime, eliminating touch-based physiological co-regulation during sleep. The evidence that night contact regulates infant physiology comes from one lab (McKenna 2014, ext 615, 616).
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable presence of nighttime body contact / proximity that preserves the touch and co-regulation channel through the sleep period; the relevant variable is continuity of contact across the 24-hour cycle, not sleep duration.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Mother and infant slept in the same room in all 173 societies of the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample and in the same bed in at least 76 (Barry and Paxson 1971). The label covers that ancestral fact only. It says nothing about the safety of bed-sharing today: the AAP 2016 guidance (room-sharing without bed-sharing) stands. The two largest case-control analyses disagree on bed-sharing where no other hazard is present: Blair et al. 2014 found no significant added risk (odds ratio 1.1), with about 18 times the risk on a sofa or beside an adult who had drunk alcohol (ext 3346); Carpenter et al. 2013 found about five times the risk for breastfed babies under 3 months whose parents neither smoke nor drink (ext 3347). On a question of an infant's life the hazard data decide, not the ancestral picture.

evidence.author_quote: Moreover, infants and mothers are induced to awaken by an arousal exhibited by the other (within seconds) therein creating interconnected, mutually dependent, synchronous arousals [1, 2].
evidence.content: Cosleeping mother and infant induce arousals in one another within seconds, creating interconnected, mutually-dependent, synchronous arousals (nighttime physiological co-regulation).

In Barry and Paxson's codes for the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, the mother slept in the same room as her infant in every one of the 173 societies coded, and in the same bed in at least 76 of them.

eea_parameters.name: Affective (C-tactile) contact frequency and skin-to-skin time
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral infants and children lived in near-continuous bodily contact: carried on the body, fed at short intervals, and held skin-to-skin for much of the day and night, with frequent affectionate, moderate-pressure touch from the mother and a wider circle of caregivers. Adults likewise lived in high-touch social fields where casual physical contact was a routine, primary channel of social interaction. Touch is the phylogenetically first and largest sense organ; the fetus is already continuously stimulated in utero. Skin-to-skin/carried contact was the species-typical default, not an intervention.

eea_value.note: No defensible single ancestral 'touches-per-hour' number; cross-cultural touch frequency ranges enormously (0-180+ contacts/hour across modern societies per Jourard), so the EEA value is a high-contact regime with a floor, not a point estimate
eea_value.infant_contact: near-continuous (carried, co-sleeping, fed at frequent short intervals)
eea_value.caregiver_scope: mother plus alloparents; high-touch social field for adults

eea_parameters.modern_default: WEIRD/industrialized environments are historically unusual in touch avoidance: infants spend much time in cribs, strollers, and carriers that minimize skin contact; personal-space norms and screen-mediated interaction strip casual affective touch from daily adult life. Many people experience chronic 'touch hunger' below the developmental and regulatory floor.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Modern environments routinely fall below the ancestral affective-touch floor. Touch deprivation in extreme cases (institutional rearing) produces growth-hormone suppression, immune dysfunction, and developmental arrest; even in non-extreme modern life the loss of moderate-pressure affective touch removes a direct oxytocin/vagal/cortisol-regulating input. Critically, affective touch is the one ancestral channel that remote, volumetric, or screen-based technology cannot deliver: it requires physical skin contact.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Reliable supply of moderate-pressure, skin-to-skin/affective (C-tactile) contact, especially in infancy and under stress; NOT incidental or light/ticklish touch (light touch does not produce the physiological response) and NOT a raw count of any contact.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Near-continuous infant carrying and frequent nursing are documented in !Kung, Aka and Efe, with breastfeeding into the second or third year across non-industrial societies (Sellen 2007). The adult high-touch part rests on modern observation and is argued. The kangaroo-care mortality benefit applies to stabilized low-birthweight infants (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; Conde-Agudelo & Diaz-Rossello 2016, ext 618) and is largest in low- and middle-income settings.

eea_parameters.name: Threat temporality (acute, episodic, escapable-by-action)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral threats were overwhelmingly acute and episodic: predators, conspecific aggression, falls, rapid environmental dangers. Each was a short, life-or-death encounter resolved within seconds-to-minutes by a discrete motor response (flee, fight, freeze, hide), after which the threat-detection system stood down and physiology returned to baseline. The fight-or-flight architecture was selected to spike hard and briefly, then terminate. Threat exposure was thus pulsatile, not continuous.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Modern stressors are chronic and non-terminating: the overbearing boss, the long commute, financial precarity, abstract status anxiety, always-on connectivity. The same stressor persists hour after hour, year after year, over a lifespan far longer than the ancestral norm, while the sympathetic/parasympathetic architecture is unchanged. The threat system is engaged at a low chronic duty cycle it was never built to sustain, and the beneficial acute response becomes damaging on the chronic timescale.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is in the time-course, not the threat machinery itself. The system is calibrated for brief, resolvable spikes; modern life supplies sustained, unresolved activation. Acute stress is adaptive (even enhances immunity); the identical response sustained chronically suppresses immunity and accumulates wear-and-tear. The gap is the absence of an episode boundary that lets the response shut down.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Calibrate to threat TEMPORALITY (episode duration and duty cycle with a terminating standdown), not threat magnitude or count. A single intense-but-resolved spike is ancestral-normal; a mild-but-unending engagement is the mismatch. The unit is 'does the activation episode end and the system return to baseline,' not 'how scary was it.'
eea_parameters.confidence_note: The acute-vs-chronic physiology is replicated in the corpus (Sapolsky id 331; McEwen id 130, both graded replicated): acute stress enhances and chronic stress suppresses immunity, and short-term vigilance changes that persist after the danger passes become maladaptive. The mismatch FRAMING (ancestral pulsatile vs modern continuous) is interpretive and rests on Cacioppo's prose (id 150, theoretical), so the row is graded argued, not yet tested, even though the underlying stress biology is well-replicated. No daily threat-frequency number is asserted. Uncontrollable threats were not rare in absolute terms. About half of forager children died before age 15 (Volk & Atkinson 2013, Evolution and Human Behavior 34(3):182-192, doi:10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2012.11.007: mean child mortality 48.8% across 20 hunter-gatherer samples, as coded by HRAF), and seasonal hunger and infectious disease were recurring threats that no individual action could resolve. The acute, controllable framing describes the typical threat episode. Uncontrollable loss was still common.

evidence.author_quote: In contemporary society, as we've noted, most of our stressors do not come and go in the kind of short, life-or-death confrontations that drove the evolution of 'fight or flight.' Moreover, we now experience these persistent stressors over a life span that, on average, extends well beyond what was the norm during all but the last few centuries of our species' existence. eea_parameters.name: What gets a person chosen, and how unequal men are
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Among foragers, men who hunted better had more surviving children (Ache, Hadza, !Kung, Lamalera, Meriam), and Hadza men with deeper voices and stronger upper bodies had more children. Hadza women put great weight on a man's foraging, and men on a woman working hard. Men's number of children varied more than women's: the male to female variance ratio was 1.66 among the Aka, 1.77 among the !Kung, 1.93 among the Hadza and 4.22 among the Ache. How large the gap is depends on the marriage system; in monogamous populations it is about 1.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Stated preferences keep the same sex differences across 45 countries (14,399 people): men weight looks and youth more, women earning prospects and an older partner. On dating sites attention concentrates on a few. In the US, the share of men aged 18 to 24 with no sex in the past year rose from 18.9% (2000 to 2002) to 30.9% (2016 to 2018), and men with lower income and no full-time work were more often sexually inactive.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Choice used to run on skill and character seen over years in a small group. On apps it runs on photos and stated traits, and the sex differences in stated preferences barely show up in whom people like when they meet. Whether the rise in sexless young men comes from this shift is untested.

The sex differences in stated preferences barely show up in whom people like when they meet (Eastwick et al. 2014, ext 757), as the gap statement states. Across 45 countries (14,399 people), gender equality was not robustly related to the sex differences in stated preferences, except for financial prospects and partner age (Walter et al. 2020, ext 695, 999); Zentner and Mitura 2012 (ext 1009) found smaller gaps with more parity across 10 nations, and 31 in a re-analysis of Buss's 1989 data. eea_parameters.name: Food diversity and seasonality (whole-food, micronutrient-dense, omnivorous variety)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral intake came from a wide, seasonally rotating array of wild plant and animal foods eaten in their whole, minimally altered form. Diet composition shifted with paleontological period, geography, and season, sustaining the broad versatility typical of an omnivore. Macronutrient and micronutrient profiles diverged sharply from the modern Western diet in nearly every measurable dimension at once: higher protein share, dramatically less refined carbohydrate and added sugar, lower sodium, higher potassium, higher micronutrient density, and near-zero industrially processed food.

eea_value.note: The 34% and 12% protein figures are model estimates (Eaton & Konner 1985, ext 39). Forager diets vary widely by habitat and season (Milton 2000, ext 763), and later reconstructions show wide ecological variation (Cordain et al. 2000, ext 729).

eea_parameters.modern_default: A narrow, year-round-uniform diet built largely from a handful of refined commodity crops (wheat, corn, soy, sugar, refined oils) recombined into processed and ultra-processed products. Seasonality is erased by global supply chains; micronutrient density falls while energy density rises; near-total replacement of whole foods with industrially formulated ones.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The modern food environment collapses a seasonally varied, micronutrient-dense, whole-food omnivory into a year-round monotony of refined, energy-dense, nutrient-diluted products, removing both the variety and the whole-food matrix the metabolic and digestive systems were calibrated to.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Whole-food matrix and dietary variety, not any single 'good' or 'bad' nutrient: the mismatch is in the wholesale shift to refined, processed forms across the whole diet, not in one macronutrient ratio.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times that forager diets varied widely with habitat and drew less energy from carbohydrate than modern diets. Strongest: two independent analyses of the ethnographic codes for 229 forager societies, Cordain et al. 2000 (ext 729: animal foods above half of subsistence in 73% of societies, protein 19 to 35% of energy) and Ströhle and Hahn 2011 (ext 3616, 3617: carbohydrate from about 3 to 50% of energy, tracking latitude and habitat, below current recommendations in most societies). Main weakness: both rest on the same coarse codes of subsistence shares, skewed toward high-latitude groups, not measured intake. Change of diet with season is measured in single populations (Hadza: Marlowe and Berbesque 2009, ext 2687). Near-zero industrial processing follows from the period. Single figures such as 34% protein are model reconstructions (Eaton and Konner 1985, ext 39) and no single value holds.

eea_parameters.name: Real-vs-perceived threat ratio and all-clear resolution
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral threat activations were predominantly responses to real, present, perceptually-verifiable dangers, and crucially each activation was terminated by an all-clear: the predator left, the danger passed, safety was confirmed. The smoke-detector logic produced many false alarms (a 1000:1 cost asymmetry makes ~999 false alarms per real escape optimal), but each alarm - true or false - was followed by behavioral resolution and a return to baseline, often reinforced by a SOCIAL all-clear (proximity, touch, return to the group), which returns the threat-responsive brain to relative calm.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Modern threats are disproportionately abstract, displaced, or symbolic (news cycles, notifications, status comparison, anticipated catastrophes) with no present referent to verify as gone and no terminating action that delivers an all-clear. The smoke-detector system keeps firing on cues it cannot resolve; social all-clear is attenuated by isolation. Activation that should be transient becomes chronic, shifting the body budget toward sustained inflammation and allostatic load.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The harmful feature is the broken resolution loop: ancestrally, alarms (real or false) closed with an all-clear; modern abstract threats supply alarms that never close. Chronically unbalanced body budgeting and unbridled inflammation are implicated in chronic stress, in persistent anxious and low states (what Western scales score as anxiety and depression), and in physical disease (Barrett; McEwen allostatic load). The mismatch is the missing terminating action and missing social all-clear, not the false-alarm rate itself - false alarms were always common and were tolerated precisely because they resolved.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Calibrate to RESOLVABILITY: a present threat that a behavioral all-clear (and a social all-clear via proximity/touch/reunion) can terminate - NOT bare threat count or alarm frequency. The ancestral system tolerated abundant false alarms; what it did not tolerate, and what modernity supplies, is alarms with no all-clear. The unit is 'can this activation be closed,' not 'how many alarms occur.'
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Strong supporting physiology: the M8 allostatic-load chain is meta_analysis (McEwen id 469) and replicated (Sapolsky id 331), and the social all-clear is replicated (Coan/SBT handholding id 125). The integrative 'real-vs-perceived ratio with missing all-clear' framing is itself an interpretive mismatch synthesis, so graded theoretical, but it is the best-evidenced of the three threat rows on the downstream-immune side. No frequency number is asserted; the high false-alarm rate is presented as ancestral-normal (id 565, theoretical signal-detection formalization), not as a defect.

eea_parameters.name: How standing is earned (prestige and dominance)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Two routes to rank exist: dominance, through fear, and prestige, through skill that others choose to defer to. In experiments with strangers both routes work. In small-scale societies prestige is the stronger route to leadership (Chabu, Tsimane), and in mobile foragers a leader's influence is informal, tied to the situation, and rests on others choosing to follow. Authority from skill stays inside the activity: Mbendjele BaYaka specialists are consulted on elephant hunting, healing or ritual and can oblige no one, and Tsimane fishing-trip organisers rotate across households and take no extra fish. Respect is different: where it was measured (one Tsimane village of 57 men, the Chabu), fighting ability, influence and respect sat with the same few men.

eea_value.tsimane_task_leaders: only 7 of 31 regular households never organised a fishing trip (von Rueden et al. 2014)

eea_parameters.modern_default: Standing is earned in large organisations and markets among people who mostly do not know each other, through titles, pay and audience size. Formal authority carries across domains: a manager commands in every part of the job, and wealth or fame buys influence outside the skill that earned it.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: In the forager record, command stayed inside the activity and could be refused; modern rank carries command across domains and is hard to refuse or leave. The concentration of respect in a few people is the part that may be old: two forager-horticulturalist samples show it.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): contested. The two-routes finding is tested many times (Cheng et al. 2013, ext 622; von Rueden et al. 2011, ext 623; Garfield and Hagen 2020, ext 624). The 'authority stays inside the activity' clause holds for command in Mbendjele BaYaka ethnography (Lewis 2014) and Tsimane task leadership (von Rueden et al. 2014) and fails for respect in a Tsimane village (von Rueden et al. 2008) and among the Chabu (ext 624). Lean: holds for command, fails for respect. Both quantitative counter-samples are semi-sedentary, which leaves room for mobile bands to differ. The modern side is described, not measured here. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 689, 732.

eea_parameters.name: Daily subsistence work-hours (contested)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: No daily work-hour figure is settled. The 'original affluent society' position (Sahlins/Lee) reads the data as short food-quest hours and ample leisure; the opposing reading (Kaplan/Hawkes/Pontzer, and Lieberman's own qualifications) emphasizes that total productive effort includes processing, childcare, toolwork, and travel, and that activity is modest-intensity but spread across the day. What the full-text evidence DOES support qualitatively is that forager workloads are not 'backbreaking' and that overall energetic activity is only modestly above a sedentary Westerner's - but this does not license any specific daily work-hour figure.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Modern work is organized around fixed, externally scheduled, often long and boundary-less hours (clock-time labor, always-on digital availability) - a structurally different time-architecture from intermittent, self-paced, weather- and resource-contingent subsistence effort, regardless of what the ancestral hour-count actually was.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The defensible mismatch is in the STRUCTURE of work-time (externally clocked, continuous, boundary-less vs. intermittent, self-paced, contingent), not in any claimed reduction or increase in daily hours.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Self-paced, resource-contingent, intermittently-bounded work time - the time ARCHITECTURE (when and how effort is scheduled and bounded), not a target number of daily hours.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): contested. Weight of evidence: once processing, travel and childcare are counted, forager work time is longer than the short-hours figures, while foragers still have more leisure than neighbouring farmers (Dyble et al. 2019); no single daily hour figure is supported.

evidence.author_quote: We find that individuals in camps engaging more in non-foraging work spend more time involved in out-of-camp work and have substantially less leisure time.
evidence.content: Across ten Agta camps whose non-foraging share of out-of-camp work ranged from 0% to 80%, a higher share of non-foraging (mostly farm) work went with less leisure (beta -0.185, 95% CI -0.35 to -0.02, P = 0.031) and more total out-of-camp work (beta 0.164, P = 0.041). The link hel
Sahlins argued that foragers met their needs with a few hours of food-getting a day and had much free time, calling them the original affluent society.

evidence.author_quote: Although there is much variation, PALs of hunter-gatherers average 1.9 for men and 1.8 for women, slightly below PAL scores for subsistence farmers, which average 2.1 for men and 1.9 for women. To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). In other words, typical hunter-gatherers are about as physically active as Americans or Europeans who include about an hour of exercise in their daily routine. In case you are wondering, most mammals in the wild have PALs of 3.3 or more, nearly twice as high as hunter-gatherers. Thus, comparatively speaking, humans who must hunt and gather all the food they eat and make everything they own by hand are substantially less active than average free-ranging mammals.
evidence.content: Physical Activity Level (PAL) data across populations reveals the surprising result that typical hunter-gatherers are only about 15% more active than industrialized people with desk jobs - equivalent to adding about an hour of exercise per day to a sedentary Westerner's routine.

evidence.author_quote: When Herman Pontzer and his colleagues measured daily energy expenditures in the Hadza, they were surprised to find that the highly active Hadza spend about the same total number of calories per day as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. In addition, when Pontzer and colleagues collected energetic data from adults in many countries including the United States, Ghana, Jamaica, and South Africa, they observed that more active people spent only slightly more calories per day than more sedentary people who weighed the same. In addition, individuals who were more physically active didn't have total energy budgets as high as their exertions would predict. How could someone who spent five hundred extra calories a day exercising not have a total energy budget that is five hundred calories higher? The proposed explanation is that people's total energy budgets are constrained: if I use five hundred extra calories walking, I'll spend less energy on my resting metabolism to help pay for my exertions.
evidence.content: The Pontzer constrained energy expenditure hypothesis: highly active Hadza spend about the same total daily energy as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. Across countries (US, Ghana, Jamaica, South Africa), more active people spend only slightly more c
Data from the Alyawara showed that once food processing is counted, foragers spent far more time on getting food than the original affluent society figures suggested.

evidence.author_quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.
evidence.content: Lieberman reports a Hadza heart-rate monitor study of 46 adults: the average adult spent about 3 h 40 min a day in light activity and 2 h 14 min in moderate or vigorous activity, which he puts at about twelve times the activity of the average American or European, and he writes t

eea_parameters.name: Size of "us" (the language group)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: A forager lived in a camp of a few dozen inside a wider group that shared a language and intermarried. Across 339 forager societies the regional ethnic unit had a geometric mean of about 840 people, with a wide spread (one standard deviation on the log scale runs from roughly 240 to 2,900). In 2012 the Eastern Hadza numbered about 950 people in 49 named bands sharing one language; the Ache tribe was defined by one language, had no tribe-wide leaders, and never gathered as a whole.

eea_value.lower_levels: family 4.5, dispersed group 15.6, aggregated camp 54, periodic gathering 165 (Hamilton et al. 2007)

eea_parameters.modern_default: People identify with nations, parties, religions and fan bases of millions, most of whose members they will never meet.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The largest group a forager counted as 'us' held hundreds to a few thousand people, reachable on foot and linked by marriage. Modern 'us' groups are thousands of times larger and held together by labels and media.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once. Strongest study: Hamilton et al. 2007 (Binford's compilation, 339 societies); one coding of what counts as a regional population, and 216 of 339 societies are North American. Hill et al. 2014 adds two populations. The nested shape is better supported than the exact size of the outer unit (EEA-SOC-01). Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 684, 754.

evidence.author_quote: We show that population structure is indeed self-similar or fractal-like with the number of individuals or groups belonging to each successively higher level of organization exhibiting a constant ratio close to 4.
evidence.content: Forager populations were organized in nested levels, with each level about three to four times larger than the one below it, from families through camps to regional groups.

evidence.author_quote: We suggest that while residential and foraging groups are often small, there is little evidence that these groups are drawn from small communities nested within small-scale societies. Most mobile hunter-gatherers live in groups dominated by links between non-relatives, where residential group membership is fluid and supports large-scale social networks of interaction
evidence.content: Forager residential groups vary widely in size and composition, and people moved between many groups across a regional network, so a single fixed small band is an oversimplification.
In Marlowe's cross-cultural sample of foragers, the median residential group size was 27 people (mean 41.4, range 13 to 250, across 263 societies).

eea_parameters.name: Wealth gaps (low to moderate in foragers)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Forager material inequality was low to moderate. Weighted wealth Gini coefficients were 0.25 for hunter-gatherers and 0.27 for horticulturalists, against 0.42 for pastoralists and 0.48 for farmers, where land and livestock can be owned and inherited (21 small-scale populations). Across eleven kinds of forager wealth most Ginis fell between 0.2 and 0.5; the two material measures averaged 0.36. House sizes at 63 archaeological sites give the same order: median Gini 0.17 at hunter-gatherer sites, 0.35 at agricultural sites.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Wealth Gini coefficients in modern states are far higher: about 0.80 for the USA in 2000 and 0.73 for China, figures Kohler et al. cite from other studies. Among the Ju/'hoansi, 44 years of cash income produced large material differences even between neighbours.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Wealth gaps went from small, mostly in body and skill, to very large, mostly in owned and inherited property, and the distance between top and bottom is now visible to everyone. Ju/'hoansi social and political equality held for decades after cash arrived, so a wealth gap does not by itself bring rule by the wealthy.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for 'forager material inequality was low to moderate'. Independent field teams (Borgerhoff Mulder et al. 2009; Smith et al. 2010) and an independent archaeological method (Kohler et al. 2017) agree. Population limit: Tsimane, Lamalera and Meriam in the ethnographic set are not mobile foragers. The modern wealth Ginis come from Davies et al. 2011 (ext 3029, 3030): 0.801 for the USA in 2000. Ju/'hoansi change: Wiessner and Huang 2022, two communities in two countries. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 756.

eea_parameters.name: Famous strangers (one-way bonds)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Everyone a forager knew of could be met. The lifetime pool of individually known people was about 1,000, and the people one heard about in stories were part of the same regional network, tied to people one knew. A person you saw and heard often knew you back.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Media supply one-way bonds with people who do not know you exist. In a quota sample of 2,028 Hungarian adults, 39% had a favourite celebrity, and on the authors' scale 4.5% of adults and 8.5% of 18 to 34 year olds had a high level of admiration. Of 151 US early adolescents, 61% thought of their favourite media figure as a relationship partner: girls mostly as a friend, boys more often as a mentor.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The bonding and status systems meet familiar, admired faces that never return the bond and never rank you. In a preregistered experiment, thinking about a favourite media figure lowered negative mood about as much as thinking about a friend, and did not lower loneliness, which thinking about a friend did (ext 1371); De Backer et al. 2007 read celebrity interest as learning from successful others plus mistaking celebrities for members of one's own network (argued).
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once, for the modern prevalence (Zsila et al. 2024, one country, cut-off set by the authors; Gleason et al. 2017, one US convenience sample). The ancestral side rests on Hill et al. 2014 (ext 606-608), one model-based study in two populations. The mismatch reading is argued, not tested. Not read: Horton and Wohl 1956, Derrick et al. 2009, Kanazawa 2002. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 1045.

evidence.author_quote: Additionally, close companions often interact with a somewhat different set of individuals, so that the total number of indirect interactants that each individual hears about repeatedly in detailed stories, and could expect to possibly meet some time during their lifetime is clearly more than 1,000. It is also much greater than the predicted 150 significant social interactants (known as “Dunbar's number”) that was extrapolated from primate brain by social group size regressions

eea_parameters.name: Contact between groups (visiting and exchange alongside hostility)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Forager bands were linked. Among the Hadza and Ache, adults who were in-laws or ritual partners interacted across bands more often, and in-law ties mattered about as much as blood ties. In 1974 each Ju/'hoansi adult kept about 15 gift-exchange partners living 2 to 200 km away and spent on average 4.4 months a year living with them. Humans form peaceful ties between groups, which chimpanzees do not. Hostility was also part of the record: the Ache and Hadza had hostile relations with neighbouring ethnic groups and no long-distance trade, and in 20 of 21 mobile forager societies about 15% of recorded killings were between groups.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Contact between large groups runs through trade, media and institutions; most members of two groups never meet, marry or visit each other.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Forager groups were tied by marriage, visits and gifts that ran through people one knew, alongside real hostility toward some neighbours. Modern intergroup ties rarely run through personal relationships.

eea_parameters.name: Killing between groups (frequency contested)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Lethal raids between groups occurred among foragers, and in some populations they were frequent. How often they happened among mobile Pleistocene foragers is not settled. Bowles compiled 23 sources and found war deaths averaged 14% of all deaths (archaeological 12%, ethnographic 16%; single sites 0% to 46%), in samples that include sedentary and contact-period groups. Fry and Soderberg found that in 21 mobile forager band societies most of 148 recorded killings had one killer and one victim; about a third were between groups, but 38 of those 50 came from one society, the Tiwi, and in the other 20 societies about 15% were. A phylogenetic estimate puts all killing by other humans at about 2% of deaths.

eea_parameters.name: What marks someone as "them" (alliance cues)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Foragers marked groups by language, dialect, ritual and marriage ties, and rarely met people genetically distant enough to look like another race. The tested part: the mind sorts people by alliance, and the sorting can be redrawn within minutes. When team membership cut across race, US participants sorted people by race less (a preregistered replication with 463 people found the drop at a smaller size; race was not erased). Arbitrary labels produce favouritism toward one's own group; a meta-analysis of cooperation experiments gives d 0.32, larger when outcomes depend on each other, and driven more by favouring 'us' than by harming 'them'.

The rise is not general: across 12 OECD democracies six saw it fall. Posts about the political out-group are shared more (each out-group word about 67% higher odds, US media and Congress). eea_parameters.gap_statement: The alliance-sorting system now runs on labels for groups of millions, with no shared life and no repeated contact, and media reward posts about 'them' (Rathje et al. 2021, eight datasets). Births were spaced about 3 to 4 years apart (hunter-gatherer average 3.7 years). About a third of forager women survived to complete their fertility. With pregnancy and long breastfeeding, menstrual cycles were few: among the Dogon, natural-fertility farmers, a woman had about 100 menstruations in her life.

eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Rates of children fathered outside the pair vary a lot between societies. In genetic studies of mostly European-descent populations, and in the Dogon of Mali, the rate is about 1 to 2%; across 67 studies the rate for men confident of their paternity was 1.9%. Within one European population over 500 years, the rate among married couples ranged from 0.4 to 5.9 percent, highest in poor families in crowded late-19th-century cities (Larmuseau et al. 2019). eea_parameters.name: Marriage system (mostly monogamous, some polygyny, serial pairs)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Most societies in the ethnographic record permitted a man more than one wife (about 85%), but in forager societies most marriages were monogamous. In 87% of 190 forager societies fewer than 20% of men were married polygynously; among tropical African foragers polygyny runs from 3% to 20%; among Savanna Pume foragers 11% of men and 20% of women are ever married polygynously. Men contributing more food went with more monogamy. Serial pairing was common: among the !Kung and Ache, men and women had children with more than one partner.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Law imposes one spouse at a time in most states (Japan from 1880, China 1953, India 1955, Nepal 1963). Serial pairing through divorce and new partners continues.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Small gap. Forager practice was already mostly one spouse at a time with some polygyny and remarriage; modern law removes the polygynous minority. Forager marriages often ended: across ten forager and forager-farmer populations reported divorce rates run from 18% (Agta) to nearly every couple (north Alaskan Inuit), and the reviewers put the general level at a quarter to a third of marriages or more, with remarriage common (ext 1728). The rates were counted differently in each population, so they cannot be averaged or set against a modern rate.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for 'mostly monogamous with some polygyny in foragers' (Apostolou coding via Walker et al. 2011; Pume demography, Schacht and Kramer 2019; African forager ethnographies via Henrich et al. 2012; Marlowe 2003, ext 767). eea_parameters.name: Who picks the partner (kin-arranged marriage)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: In most forager societies parents or close kin arranged marriages. In Apostolou's coding of 190 forager societies, arrangement by parents or close kin was the main way to marry in 85%, and marriage involved an exchange between the two families (brideservice, brideprice) in 80%. A phylogenetic reconstruction puts arranged marriage at least as far back as the migrations out of Africa. Courtship also existed: 3 of the 8 African forager societies in the sample marry by courtship, so the oldest African pattern is open. eea_parameters.name: Leadership and dominance (no rulers; prestige by consent; exit available)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Mobile hunter-gatherer bands had no rulers. Decisions that affected the group were reached by discussion toward consensus. Influence came from prestige and lasted only while others chose to listen. Anyone who tried to dominate was mocked, shunned or expelled, and in extreme cases killed. People could also leave a camp for another one, and that option checked anyone who tried to take control.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Rulers are chosen at state scale. The people who hold power are personally unknown to almost everyone they govern, and the polity is in practice impossible to leave.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The forager checks on dominance (ridicule, shunning, walking away, a voice in a face-to-face decision) have no reach over rulers who never meet the people they govern. One person's say shrinks from a share of a camp consensus to one vote among millions.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times for mobile foragers. Mobile foragers suppress would-be dominants and leaders rule by consent across the ethnographic record (Boehm 1993, ext 688; Garfield, von Rueden and Hagen 2019, ext 689); main weakness: the ethnographies differ in method and date. Singh and Glowacki 2022 (ext 756) review 34 regions and argue that sedentary, unequal non-agricultural societies also existed through the Late Pleistocene; their data are mostly sedentary Holocene societies, and they do not dispute the description of mobile foragers. The baseline describes mobile, immediate-return foragers (Woodburn 1982, ext 677). Mbendjele BaYaka mock men who hunt a lot and in effect exiled one persistent hunter; braggarts are teased, avoided and if they persist exiled (Lewis 2014, ext 848). Tsimane fishing-trip organisers rotate across households and take no more fish than others (von Rueden et al. 2014, ext 1038). Ju/'hoansi kept social, gender and political equality for decades after cash created large wealth gaps (Wiessner and Huang 2022, ext 1034). Wealth inequality itself: EEA-SOC-14.

eea_parameters.name: Dawn/dusk light gradient with genuine nocturnal darkness as circadian entrainment signal
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Across evolutionary history the human circadian pacemaker (suprachiasmatic nucleus) was entrained by a high-amplitude natural light-dark cycle: bright full-spectrum daytime illumination (often >10,000 lux outdoors), a gradual dusk dimming and reddening, and then real darkness for the duration of the biological night, with only firelight (low, long-wavelength) as evening illumination. Contemporary hunter-gatherer reference populations (Hadza, San) show sleep onset clustering around 8-10 p.m., aligned with dusk-driven melatonin release. The operative signal is the timing and spectral content of light at the day-night transition reaching melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells, not light intensity per se.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Indoor electric and screen light keeps evening illumination bright and short-wavelength (blue-enriched, ~450nm) well past dusk, suppressing melatonin and delaying its onset by 1.5-3 hours; daytime indoor light is far dimmer than outdoor light, flattening the day-night amplitude. The dusk dimming/reddening gradient and true nocturnal darkness are largely abolished.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The modern light environment inverts the ancestral pattern on both ends: too little bright light by day, too much blue-enriched light at night, with no real darkness. This delays circadian phase, compresses and fragments the biological night, and decouples internal time from external solar time.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Spectral timing of light exposure at the day-night transition (dusk dimming + nocturnal darkness), not total daily light dose or generic 'brightness'.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Pre-electric light exposure and sleep timing are measured in Hadza, San and Tsimane (Yetish et al. 2015), in Toba/Qom with and without electricity (de la Iglesia et al. 2015) and in natural-light camping studies; samples are small and modern foragers stand in for ancestral ones. Sleep onset averaged about 3.3 hours after sunset in Yetish et al. In about 400,000 UK adults, each extra hour a day outdoors in daylight went with less frequent low mood and tiredness, fewer insomnia symptoms, an earlier chronotype and lower odds of antidepressant use (Burns et al. 2021).

evidence.content: Electric light, caffeine, and alarm clocks systematically disrupt the ancestral dark-cycle sleep pattern that governed human circadian biology for millennia. Walker describes how Edison's incandescent light "put an end to this natural order of things," delaying melatonin release

evidence.content: The circadian rhythm - the twenty-four-hour biological pacemaker - orchestrates mood, metabolic timing, hormonal release, body temperature, and cognitive performance. The suprachiasmatic nucleus generates this rhythm and is synchronized by light-dark cycles. Artificial lighting,
