evidence.author_quote: Here we show that electrical lighting and the constructed environment is associated with reduced exposure to sunlight during the day, increased light exposure after sunset, and a delayed timing of the circadian clock as compared to a summer natural 14h40min:9h20min light-dark cycle camping. Furthermore, we find that after exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time such that the beginning of the internal biological night occurs at sunset and the end of the internal biological night occurs before wake time just after sunrise.
evidence.content: After exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time: biological night begins at sunset and ends just after sunrise; electrical lighting is associated with a delayed clock.

evidence.author_quote: Following the week of exposure to natural lighting, all measured markers of internal circadian time were ~2h earlier (Fig 3., all p<0.01; Bonferroni correction required p<0.0167, one tailed) and remarkably, melatonin onset occurred on average near sunset, the melatonin midpoint occurred in the middle of the solar night, and melatonin offset occurred before wake time just after sunrise. Sleep timing was related to circadian timing after electrical lighting-constructed conditions and less so after exposure to only natural light (Supplemental information Table S1 and Fig. S2). The advance in timing of melatonin onset was significantly larger than changes in sleep start and wake times which changed by ~1.2h (Fig. 3, both p<0.02; Bonferroni correction required p<0.025, two tailed). Weekly sleep duration (6.7±0.9h electrical versus 6.8h±0.7h natural lighting; p=0.268, twotailed) and sleep efficiency (87.6±5.6% electrical versus 87.0±4.6% natural lighting; p=0.49, two-tailed) did not significantly change indicating that a change in sleep amount or efficiency did not contribute to the current findings.
evidence.content: One week of natural light advanced all circadian markers ~2h (melatonin onset near sunset) while sleep duration and efficiency were statistically unchanged: the change was in circadian PHASE/timing, not sleep amount.

evidence.author_quote: Natural sunlight is a stronger environmental zeitgeber or time cue for the internal circadian clock than is electrical lighting in the constructed environment.
evidence.content: Natural sunlight is a stronger circadian zeitgeber than electrical lighting in the constructed environment.

evidence.author_quote: We have previously shown that exposure to a natural summer 14 hr 40 min:9 hr 20 min light-dark cycle entrains the human circadian clock to solar time, such that the internal biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise [1]. Here we show the beginning of the biological night and sleep occur earlier after a week exposure to a natural winter 9 hr 20 min:14 hr 40 min light-dark cycle as compared to the modern electrical lighting environment.
evidence.content: Replicates and extends Wright 2013: natural light entrains the clock so the biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise; under a natural WINTER light-dark cycle the biological night and sleep occur earlier than under modern electrical lighting.

evidence.author_quote: others have reported later circadian and/or sleep timing in Brazilian rubber tappers [2] and in hunter-gatherers from the indigenous Toba/Qom in the Argentinean Chaco with access to electrical lighting compared to those from the same communities without access to electrical lighting
evidence.content: Convergent field evidence: indigenous Toba/Qom hunter-gatherers and Brazilian rubber-tappers WITH electrical lighting show later circadian/sleep timing than same-community members WITHOUT it.

evidence.content: Among the Ju/'hoansi, daytime talk was mostly about economic matters, complaints and gossip, while firelight talk at night was mostly stories.

eea_parameters.name: Daily incidental movement load
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Across a foraging day, adults covered substantial ground on foot as a structural side-effect of acquiring food, water, and firewood and of moving between patches and camp: Hadza men walk about 11.4 km a day and women about 5.8 km, and the women also dig for several hours (Pontzer et al. 2012, GPS; ext 196). Movement was woven through the whole waking day rather than concentrated into a bout. Activity was modest in intensity but near-continuous and embedded: light chores, child-carrying, frequent sit-to-stand transitions, and active resting postures (squatting, kneeling) that sustain low-level lower-limb muscle activity. Hunter-gatherer PAL is only modestly above a Western desk worker's (~1.8-1.9 vs ~1.6), so the EEA baseline is not 'extreme exertion' but 'movement is the unavoidable medium of subsistence.'

daily_distance_km.source: Pontzer et al. 2012, PLoS ONE, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0040503 (GPS means)
daily_distance_km.qualifier: Hadza only; a side effect of the foraging day

rest_hours_per_day.note: comparable to industrialized adults; difference is posture not amount

eea_parameters.modern_default: Movement has been extracted from subsistence and re-inserted, if at all, as discretionary 'exercise': set-aside, planned, dose-prescribed (e.g. 150 min/week guidelines), and separated from the rest of a chair-bound, motor-transported, indoor day. Most waking hours are spent in continuous chair-sitting that holds the lower limbs near-inactive, and total daily distance on foot collapses far below the ancestral range.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The gap is not a calorie or PAL gap (these are surprisingly close) but a distributional one: ancestral movement was low-intensity, continuous, and obligatory; modern movement is optional, bunched, and easily skipped, leaving long uninterrupted muscular-inactivity bouts that the body never encountered. The mismatch is in HOW the day's muscle activity is spread, not in gross energy turnover.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Incidental all-day movement woven into the fabric of living (errands, carrying, standing, walking between activities, active rest postures) - NOT a set-aside 'exercise' session. The functional target is the continuous distribution of low-level activity across waking hours, not weekly minutes of vigorous training.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Forager activity of over 100 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous movement and activity levels modestly above Western ones are found across populations (Pontzer, Wood and Raichlen 2018); the kilometre and rest figures are Hadza only.

evidence.author_quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.
evidence.content: Lieberman reports a Hadza heart-rate monitor study of 46 adults: the average adult spent about 3 h 40 min a day in light activity and 2 h 14 min in moderate or vigorous activity, which he puts at about twelve times the activity of the average American or European, and he writes t

evidence.content: Modern sedentary lifestyle is directly mismatched with ancestral activity patterns. Walking 9 (women) to 15 (men) kilometers daily when foraging, climbing trees, throwing, eschewing chairs, and sleeping on hard surfaces were normal for most of human evolutionary history. The prim

evidence.author_quote: Although there is much variation, PALs of hunter-gatherers average 1.9 for men and 1.8 for women, slightly below PAL scores for subsistence farmers, which average 2.1 for men and 1.9 for women. To put these values into context, hunter-gatherer PALs are about the same as those of factory workers and farmers in the developed world (1.8), and about 15 percent higher than PALs of people with desk jobs in developed countries (1.6). In other words, typical hunter-gatherers are about as physically active as Americans or Europeans who include about an hour of exercise in their daily routine. In case you are wondering, most mammals in the wild have PALs of 3.3 or more, nearly twice as high as hunter-gatherers. Thus, comparatively speaking, humans who must hunt and gather all the food they eat and make everything they own by hand are substantially less active than average free-ranging mammals.
evidence.content: Physical Activity Level (PAL) data across populations reveals the surprising result that typical hunter-gatherers are only about 15% more active than industrialized people with desk jobs - equivalent to adding about an hour of exercise per day to a sedentary Westerner's routine.

evidence.author_quote: Here, we test the hypothesis that the ways in which urban populations rest, rather than the amount of time spent resting, represents an inactivity mismatch with an evolutionarily relevant hunting and gathering lifestyle, and propose that this mismatch may contribute to the negative health impacts of sedentary behavior today.
evidence.content: The Inactivity Mismatch Hypothesis (Raichlen, Pontzer et al. 2020): Hadza adults spend similar amounts of time in nonambulatory rest as industrialized adults (~9.9 hours/day), but much of that rest is in postures - squatting and kneeling - that maintain higher lower-limb muscle a

[...] For soleus, the assisted squat posture (squatting with heels in ground contact and with the buttocks resting on a small rock) elicited significantly higher muscle activity compared with chair sitting.

evidence.author_quote: My opinion is that while many animals are driven by deep instincts to move, sometimes causing pleasure, exercise as we define it - discretionary, planned physical activity for the sake of physical improvement - is a uniquely human behavior. In fact, I think it is fair to make two generalizations about human exercise. First, while youngsters have always played and sports are a human universal, exercise outside the context of sports was extremely rare until relatively recently. Second, as recent technological and social developments have diminished industrialized people's need to be physically active, a growing chorus of experts has never ceased to raise the alarm that we aren't exercising enough.

evidence.author_quote: Many things surprised me when I first walked into a Hadza camp mid-morning on a torrid, sunny day in 2013, but I remember being especially struck by how everyone was apparently doing nothing. Hadza camps consist of a few temporary grass huts that blend in with the surrounding bushes. I didn't realize I had walked into a camp until I found myself amid about fifteen Hadza men, women, and children who were sitting on the ground as shown in figure 2. The women and children were relaxing on one side, and the men on another. One fellow was straightening some arrows, and a few children were toddling about, but no one was engaged in any hard work. To be sure, the Hadza weren't lounging on sofas, watching TV, munching potato chips, and sipping soda, but they were doing what so many health experts warn us to avoid: sitting.

eea_parameters.name: Threat controllability and predictability (resolvable by own action)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral threats were typically controllable and predictable in the relevant sense: the animal's own behavior (run, climb, hide, defend, call allies) reliably altered the outcome, and the threat's presence/absence was perceptually verifiable. Uncontrollable, action-proof stressors were the rare, extreme case. The threat system evolved on the expectation that vigilance would be followed by an effective response that resolves the danger.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Many modern stressors are structurally uncontrollable and unpredictable: algorithmic management and electronic monitoring strip decision latitude, outcomes hinge on systems no single action can move, and dread is open-ended (an unknown deadline, an unbounded threat). No behavior reliably terminates the stressor, producing the conditions for learned helplessness and chronic anticipatory dread.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The harm comes from uncontrollability and unpredictability, the absence of an action that resolves the danger, more than from threat itself. Lab work shows lack of predictability and control is so aversive that subjects choose a stronger immediate shock over waiting, and chronic uncontrollable stress reproduces eight of the nine symptoms the DSM lists for depression. Modern environments systematically supply unresolvable, action-proof stressors - the mismatch.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Calibrate to CONTROLLABILITY = whether a behavioral response reliably terminates or averts the threat, not to mere familiarity or low intensity. A predictable-but-uncontrollable stressor (you see it coming, nothing you do helps) is the toxic case; an unfamiliar-but-action-resolvable one is ancestral-normal.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: The controllability/predictability physiology is replicated (Sapolsky id 333; learned-helplessness id 442, both graded replicated). The EEA-baseline claim that ancestral threats were predominantly controllable is interpretive (no extraction quantifies ancestral controllability), so graded argued, not yet tested, with the underlying control science noted as replicated. Uncontrollable threats were not rare in absolute terms. About half of forager children died before age 15 (Volk & Atkinson 2013, Evolution and Human Behavior 34(3):182-192, doi:10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2012.11.007: mean child mortality 48.8% across 20 hunter-gatherer samples, as coded by HRAF), and seasonal hunger and infectious disease were recurring threats that no individual action could resolve. The acute, controllable framing describes the typical threat episode. Uncontrollable loss was still common.

evidence.author_quote: In another study subjects waited an unknown length of time to receive a shock. This lack of predictability and control was so aversive that many chose to receive a stronger shock immediately. And in the others the period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.
evidence.content: Lack of predictability and control over stressors is so aversive that many subjects chose to receive a stronger shock immediately rather than wait an unknown time for a weaker one. The period of anticipatory dread increasingly activated the amygdala.

eea_parameters.name: Relationship longevity & maintenance (decades-long durable dyads; ~27-yr co-survival ceiling; maintenance institutions like hxaro conserve bonds across distance)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: In ancestral foraging life the load-bearing social unit was the durable, reciprocal DYAD, not the group. Because groups continuously reshuffled (camps fissioned/fused on the order of every ~4-8 weeks, with most campmates changing from one survey wave to the next), what was conserved across the churn was the relationship itself, sustained for decades by both face-to-face co-presence when proximity allowed AND by explicit maintenance institutions when it did not. Among the Ju/'hoansi, hxaro was a formal delayed-reciprocity gift-partnership system reported to begin in childhood, be kept for life, be inherited at death, and span dispersed bands up to ~200 km apart, with only a minority of a person's partners co-resident in the current camp, so a bond could persist even when the two partners were rarely or never in the same camp. Two adults who reached adulthood together could expect on the order of ~27 years of overlapping co-survival, and reciprocal alliances ran over that whole horizon. Trivers's conditions for the evolution of reciprocal altruism describe exactly this regime: a long lifetime, low dispersal, and repeated interaction with the same small set of individuals, so that an investment in a specific partner reliably paid back over time.

eea_value._note: The 200 km hxaro range and about 15 partners per adult come from Wiessner & Huang 2022 (ext 752; Ju/'hoansi, 1974). The ~27-year co-survival figure, the ~18% co-resident figure, and childhood onset and inheritance are attributed to Wiessner 2002, which is not in Cor and has not been read. For turnover: no number is used; see campmate_turnover_status. Camps shift every ~4-8 weeks (Smith et al. 2018, core work 116).
eea_value.campmate_turnover_status: UNVERIFIED: see EEA-SOC-05. Smith et al. 2018 (Hadza; in Cor as core work 116) preprint v1 reports 12.1% repeated campmates and v2 reports 21.9%, under different definitions; survey waves are 1 to 3 years apart, so neither is an annual rate; the published figure was not read.

eea_parameters.modern_default: The modern environment inverts the ancestral pattern: it supplies stable GROUP labels (a workplace, a school cohort, a social-media feed, a city) while the dyads inside them are shallow and disposable, and there is no institutional equivalent of hxaro that conserves a specific bond once physical proximity ends. When two people stop sharing a context, the relationship is simply allowed to decay; nothing structurally obligates either party to keep servicing it. Empirically, friendships require recurring face-to-face contact to avoid sliding down through the network layers and eventually dropping out of the personal network entirely, and online media at best slows that decay rather than preventing it. Trust and bond depth track time invested in a relationship, and the maintenance cost (mainly time) scales roughly linearly with the number of relationships, so modern people spread thin investment across large, low-trust networks and let most ties lapse rather than maintaining a small set of partners across decades.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The ancestral environment conserved the relationship across changing groups; the modern environment conserves the group label and lets the relationships churn. The specific missing piece is a maintenance institution: the EEA had hxaro-type structures (formalized, inheritable, distance-spanning, long-term delayed reciprocity) that actively preserved a named dyad even with little or no co-presence, whereas modernity has no hxaro-equivalent and instead relies on shared proximity/context as the only glue. When that proximity ends (job change, move, leaving school), the bond is not migrated to an institution that keeps it alive; it decays. The result is many stable-looking memberships sitting on top of disposable, shallow ties, with the durable decades-long reciprocal partnership that M3/M11 are calibrated to expect largely absent.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: The durable, spatially-dispersed reciprocal DYAD plus the maintenance institutions that conserve it across distance and time - i.e., a specific named partner whose bond is actively serviced (face-to-face when possible, and via hxaro-type delayed-reciprocity exchange when apart) so the relationship persists for decades and survives the reshuffling of any particular group. Conserved across the churn is the relationship, not the group; the resolution requires migrating a bond to an institution that keeps it alive once proximity ends, not merely accumulating more low-investment ties.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade: tested once. Hxaro range and partner count: Wiessner & Huang 2022 (ext 752), Ju/'hoansi only. Co-survival and co-resident figures: Wiessner 2002, not in Cor and unread. Camps move every 4 to 8 weeks (Smith et al. 2018, ext 604, Hadza), and no turnover number is used (see EEA-SOC-05). Modern side: Dunbar proposes that friendships decay without face-to-face meetings and that social media only slow the decay (Dunbar 2016, ext 509, 510; cross-sectional data). In the model of Sutcliffe et al. 2012, the time cost of keeping relationships grows in line with their number, and trust grows with time invested (ext 503, 505; theoretical). Reciprocity is favoured by a long lifetime, low dispersal and repeated interaction with the same few individuals (Trivers 1971, ext 479).

eea_parameters.name: Energy regulation is intake-bounded (total expenditure is homeostatically buffered, not behavior-throttled)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Total daily energy expenditure (TEE) is an evolved, species-typical trait that the body holds within a narrow range, compensating metabolically rather than expending proportionally more as physical activity rises. Hunter-gatherers and subsistence populations expend about the same total daily energy as industrialized adults of the same body size despite far greater physical activity; the same wild-vs-captive constancy appears across mammals. Ancestrally, the binding constraint on energy balance was therefore food INTAKE (how much could be acquired and its composition), not how many calories activity could burn off.

eea_value.finding: TEE constant across activity levels after controlling for body size
eea_value.implication: Obesity difference between Hadza and Westerners lies in intake/composition, not in expenditure.

eea_parameters.modern_default: The dominant lay (and much policy) model treats body weight as 'calories in minus calories out' with exercise as the lever for the 'out' side. Because expenditure is homeostatically buffered, this model fails: cranking up activity yields little net caloric deficit, while the intake side - driven by hyperpalatable, energy-dense, effortless food - is what has changed and what dysregulates energy balance.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Modern environments leave intake unbounded (cheap, hyperpalatable, effortless calories) while the body's expenditure stays homeostatically capped - so the one variable the system relied on as the binding constraint (limited, worked-for food) is exactly the one industrialization removed, and the popular 'just exercise it off' remedy targets the wrong, buffered side.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: The binding constraint on energy balance: ancestrally INTAKE (food availability/composition), not expenditure. The mismatch is unbounded intake, not insufficient calorie-burning; exercise is a weak proxy for the metabolic problem.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade: tested many times. Total energy expenditure rises with activity at low levels and plateaus above moderate activity in doubly-labelled-water data from five populations (Pontzer et al. 2016, n=332, ext 283). Foragers and subsistence farmers expend about as much energy as people in industrial populations, and wild mammals about as much as captive ones (ext 284). The Hadza study found the same daily expenditure as in Western adults after controlling for body size (Pontzer et al. 2012, n=30, ext 286), which places the obesity difference in intake and food composition, and it proposes that daily energy expenditure is an evolved trait (ext 287). In trials, aerobic exercise alone took off 1.6 kg against controls at 6 months (14 trials, ext 3594), and 3.9 and 5.2 kg under 10 months of supervised sessions five days a week (Donnelly et al. 2013, ext 4028). The achieved energy deficit was in most trials smaller than the energy the sessions burned, mostly because people ate more (Thomas et al. 2012, ext 4054); with intake held fixed, resting metabolic rate fell about 7 percent beyond what the weight lost accounts for (ext 4055).

evidence.author_quote: As expected, physical activity level, PAL, was greater among Hadza foragers than among Westerners. Nonetheless, average daily energy expenditure of traditional Hadza foragers was no different than that of Westerners after controlling for body size. The metabolic cost of walking and resting were also similar among Hadza and Western groups. The similarity in metabolic rates across a broad range of cultures challenges current models of obesity suggesting that Western lifestyles lead to decreased energy expenditure.
evidence.content: The Pontzer 2012 Hadza-energetics finding: despite greater physical activity (Hadza PAL ~1.78-2.26 vs Western PAL ~1.68-1.81), Hadza hunter-gatherers expend no more total daily energy than Western adults after controlling for body size. The metabolic cost of walking and resting a

evidence.author_quote: Here we tested a Constrained total energy expenditure model, in which total energy expenditure increases with physical activity at low activity levels but plateaus at higher activity levels as the body adapts to maintain total energy expenditure within a narrow range. We compared total energy expenditure, measured using doubly labeled water, against physical activity, measured using accelerometry, for a large (n = 332) sample of adults living in five populations. eea_parameters.name: Food shared and eaten in company
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: In every forager group with a record, food moved between households. A review of 45 small-scale groups reports food transfers beyond the household throughout, and in all 10 groups where it was checked big game reached more families than small game. Among the Hadza of Tanzania at least 90% of the meat of large animals left the hunter's household. Among the Aka of the Congo a cook and her children ate about 20% of the stew she made, about 75% of the stew a woman ate came from other women's pots, cooking and serving were done in plain view, and the men usually ate together at the men's shelter. Among the Ju/'hoansi of Botswana each family ate the evening meal at its own fire and people then gathered at shared fires. Among the Great Andamanese game was roasted at a public cooking place and each family ate at its own hut. Batek camps in Malaysia, about 34 people, shared food at once, stored none and ate almost nothing out of camp. Hadza men ate on the foray, out of camp, about 90 percent of what they are estimated to spend in a day, most of it honey (ext 3162). The meal was mostly a family meal, eaten in sight and reach of the rest of the camp. No record shows a whole camp eating as one table every day. Sharing with the whole band was the exception and went with bands under 40 to 50 people.
eea_parameters.modern_default: In the United States 26% of adults ate every meal of the previous day alone in 2023, more than half again above the 2003 level; among people living alone it was about 70%. In a UK poll of 2,000 adults nearly 70% had never had a meal with a neighbour. Shared meals vary widely between countries today: 11.7 lunches and dinners a week with someone known in Senegal, 2.7 in Bangladesh and Estonia. Food now comes from a shop, and a household's food does not pass through other households.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: A forager ate food that others in the camp had caught, carried or cooked, and others ate theirs, among people who knew who gave what. A person who eats alone from a shop gets the calories without the giving and receiving. Project position: the missing exchange is what lowers mood. Among 37,193 older Japanese adults followed for three years, men living alone who usually ate alone had 2.36 times the rate of new depressive symptoms of men living alone who ate with others, after adjustment for income, health, nutrition and other factors (ext 3684); in a cross-sectional study, people who lived with their families yet ate alone had the highest odds of depressive symptoms (ext 3583).

That food reaches other households is tested many times: it is reported in every one of the 45 small-scale groups in Gurven's review (ext 1577). Who ate whose cooked food has been counted once. Strongest study: Kitanishi 1998 (ext 1586), 103 days of counts in two Aka camps; main weakness: one ethnographer in one region, and the 20% and 75% figures rest on his estimate of what stayed in the pot. Modern side: the US time-use series (De Neve et al. 2025, ext 1603); main weakness: one country, in a report chapter without journal review. The links between shared meals and life ratings (ext 1602, 1604) are cross-sectional and both sources leave the direction open. Sharing was also unequal and sometimes followed a demand; none of this goes against the row, since the food still moved between households among people who knew who gave what. Producers often kept more than an equal share (ext 1578), Hadza hunters' households were favoured in later data (ext 828), and Peterson argues that much sharing follows a demand (ext 709, 1580); Altman, who reports most sharing within the household, gives no counts (ext 1581), and among the Aka people avoided asking (ext 1588).

eea_parameters.name: Social network layers (~5/15/50/150)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: The ancestral social world was structured as a series of hierarchically inclusive, nested relationship layers, each roughly three times the size of the one inside it: an innermost support clique of ~5 close confidants who provided emotional and physical support, a sympathy group of ~15 (people whose loss would be deeply felt, contacted at least monthly), an affinity/band layer of ~50 (the typical overnight foraging camp of casual-but-close associates), and an active personal network of ~150 (the clan/tribal layer, the outer ceiling of stable, individually-known relationships). Each layer carried a qualitatively different grade of intimacy, obligation, and contact frequency, with the heaviest investment concentrated in the inner ~5-15. The ~150 outer figure is an illustrative central tendency, not a constant: traditional tribal and clan groupings cluster in the low hundreds. Its original derivation from the primate neocortex-ratio regression fails re-analysis (Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind 2021), so the specific number is treated as approximate; what is load-bearing is the nested layering, not the precise ceiling. This was the full architecture within which status was monitored and alliances tracked: a personally-known reference group bounded at ~150, not an anonymous mass.

eea_value.outer_ceiling_note: low hundreds; ~150 is an approximate central tendency, not a constant; the neocortex-ratio derivation is contested (Lindenfors 2021)

eea_parameters.modern_default: The modern environment delivers a radically inverted network shape: nominal friend/follower counts in the hundreds or thousands that vastly exceed the ~150 cognitive ceiling, while the layers that actually carry support and intimacy stay capacity-bounded. Online networks reproduce the same ~5/15 inner structure when genuine ties are measured (support clique ~4, sympathy group ~14, statistically indistinguishable from offline values), and mean platform friend counts hover near ~150-190 (across all 721 million Facebook users of May 2011 the mean was about 190 and the median 99; Ugander et al. 2011, ext 4624), but the bulk of nominal connections are inactive labels rather than relationships (only ~27.6% of online 'friends' are reported as genuine). Inner-layer bonds decay back toward mere acquaintance without the face-to-face contact the architecture was built to expect; mediated contact slows but does not substitute for it. The result is a wide, shallow periphery of weak or fictive ties layered on top of a core that the larger network does not, and cannot, enlarge: among 117 adults, more time on social media went with more online friends and with no larger or emotionally closer offline network (Pollet, Roberts and Dunbar 2011).
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is not in the inner-layer capacities themselves (still ~5/15/50/150, not technologically expandable) but between the number of ties the modern environment presents (hundreds to thousands of nominal contacts) and the number the brain can actually monitor and invest in (~150, with real support concentrated in the inner ~5-15). People with unusually large networks do not gain more close friends; they accumulate weakly-defined acquaintances. Status monitoring (M5) and alliance/reputation tracking (M11), evolved for a ~150 personally-known reference group, are now flooded by reference groups orders of magnitude larger and largely composed of strangers, while the trust-bearing inner layers remain capped and are under-fed when face-to-face contact is displaced.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times for the layering. Forager populations were organised in nested levels, each about three to four times the size of the one below, across 339 societies in Binford's compilation (Hamilton et al. 2007, ext 1048: families of about 4.5, dispersed groups of 15.6, residential groups of 54, periodic gatherings of 165). Personal networks fall into nested layers about three times the size of the one inside in pooled published group sizes (Zhou et al. 2005, ext 2042), phone records of 34.9 million users (Mac Carron, Kaski and Dunbar 2016, ext 2026), and Facebook and Twitter contact data (Dunbar et al. 2015, ext 4336; Arnaboldi et al. 2016, ext 3323). A model with one fixed capacity for relationships, in which closer ties cost more, reproduces the layers, and about 98 percent of 84 students' networks showed them with a scaling ratio of about 2.7 to 3.1 (Tamarit et al. 2018). Main weakness: the forager levels are group sizes, not one person's network, and the modern network data all come from Dunbar's group and its collaborators. The 150 figure fails re-analysis of the primate regression it came from (Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind 2021, ext 619), so the layer sizes and the 150 ceiling are approximate. Forager residential groups are fluid (Bird et al. 2019, ext 684), which concerns who shares a camp, not the layers of a person's network.

eea_parameters.name: Behavioral observability / reputation visibility
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: In a band/camp embedded in a personally-known reference group of roughly 150 individuals, virtually all of a person's relevant behavior was directly observable by, or rapidly transmitted through gossip to, people who knew them by name, knew their history, and would interact with them again for decades. Reputation was a shared, continuously-updated, distributed record: as Boehm puts it, "the band keeps a dossier on every individual, noting positive and negative points." Where campmates differed, they knew it: asked one by one in 12 Hadza camps, they agreed more on who hunts best (r 0.23) and a little more on who works hardest (r 0.08). They barely agreed on who shares the most food, who tells the fewest lies and who has the best heart (ext 2795). Project position (21 Nov 2026): anyone still in camp shared and was honest enough to be kept there, so on those points there was little left to rank, and such labels sort strangers more than campmates. The study's authors read the low agreement as moral behaviour that changes across time and situations to fit local circumstances (ext 2796). Observability had teeth: those who deviated (theft, deception, stinginess, free-riding) were subject to gossip, ridicule, ostracism, and ultimately exclusion, and everyone knew this monitoring was constant, so it functioned as a deterrent and people exercised self-control accordingly. Because foraging was obligately collaborative, individuals had to continuously evaluate partners and track how they themselves were being evaluated. The net result: visibility was near-total, embodied, hard to fake over time, attached to a single durable identity, and backed by real consequences enforced by people one could not escape.

eea_value.identity: single durable identity, behavior history attached for life
eea_value.observability: near-total within band/camp; rapid gossip diffusion across the ~150 layer
eea_value.accountability: high: gossip, ridicule, ostracism, exclusion; non-exitable repeat interaction
eea_value.reference_group_basis: personally-known, named, repeat-interaction reference group (Dunbar ceiling)

eea_parameters.modern_default: Most behavior now occurs among strangers or weak ties who do not know one's history and will never interact with one again, while the visibility that does exist is mediated, curated, and quantitatively inflated. On social platforms only ~27.6% of nominal "friends" are considered genuine close ties (with a strong modal value between 0 and 10%), so networks are padded with weakly-accountable acquaintances rather than people tracking one's actual conduct. Mediated contact cannot substitute for the embodied, face-to-face observation the bonding/reputation system evolved for: without periodic in-person contact, ties decay through the network layers into mere acquaintance regardless of online activity. Visibility is now selectively self-presented (gameable), fragmented across multiple personas and contexts, frequently pseudonymous or low-stakes, and policed (if at all) by distant institutions or algorithms rather than by named peers with whom one shares a future. Reputation is either absent (anonymity), sortable away (exit/blocking, fresh accounts), or captured by platform metrics that reward performance over honesty.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The ancestral environment delivered near-total, embodied, hard-to-fake, single-identity behavioral observability inside a ~150-person reference group whose members knew one's history and held real, inescapable enforcement power. The modern environment delivers visibility that is mediated, curated, gameable, fragmented across exitable contexts, padded with non-accountable weak ties, and largely stripped of peer-enforced consequences. The reputation-tracking machinery (M11) and status-position monitoring (M5) evolved to run on dense, durable, accountable observation now operate on thin, performative, low-accountability signals, producing both reputational impunity for defection among strangers and chronic exposure of curated personas to vast unfamiliar audiences with no reciprocal knowledge of the person behind them.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade: argued, not yet tested. Forager bands track reputation through gossip, ridicule and ostracism (Boehm 1999, ext 373, 375), and partners evaluate each other (Tomasello 2014, ext 239). The threat of gossip made people more generous in experiments (Feinberg et al. 2012, ext 719), and in 15 small-scale communities shame tracked how much the community would devalue an act (Sznycer et al. 2018, ext 722). Modern side: respondents counted only 27.6% of their Facebook friends as genuine (Dunbar 2016, ext 508), and Dunbar proposes that ties decay without face-to-face meetings (ext 509; cross-sectional data). Two meta-analyses found no evidence that artificial watching-eye cues raise generosity (Northover et al. 2017, ext 829). No study compares ancestral and modern observability directly. The comparison is the framework's reading.

evidence.author_quote: In the hypothesis of Tomasello et al. (2012), obligate collaborative foraging became an evolutionarily stable strategy for early humans because of two interrelated processes: interdependence and social selection. The first and most basic point is that humans began a lifestyle in which individuals could not procure their daily sustenance alone but instead were interdependent with others in their foraging activities - which meant that individuals needed to develop the skills and motivations to forage collaboratively or else starve. There was thus direct and immediate selective pressure for skills and motivations for joint collaborative activity (joint intentionality). The second point is that as a natural outcome of this interdependence, individuals began to make evaluative judgments about others as potential collaborative partners: they began to be socially selective, since choosing a poor partner meant less food. Cheaters and laggards were thus selected against, and bullies lost their power to bully.

eea_parameters.name: Satiety-honest fiber and whole-food matrix (food that signals fullness truthfully)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Ancestral foods were fibrous, water- and bulk-rich, and slow to eat and digest, so the volume and macronutrient signals reaching satiety circuits tracked the actual caloric load. Reconstructions place ancestral fiber intake far above modern levels (on the order of 100 g/day or somewhat more vs ~20 g today; Eaton 2006, ext 3605). Sweetness, fat, and salt arrived bundled inside a whole-food matrix; sweet food was seasonal and costly to obtain (for the Hadza, honey is a favourite food and a substantial calorie share in season, Marlowe et al. 2014), and fat and salt came at concentrations that were ancestrally rare, so the reward-system's responses to those cues were honest proxies for nutritional value.

eea_value.note: Fiber figures are reconstructions (Eaton 2006, ext 3605, which lowered the 100 to 150 g of Eaton & Konner 1985, ext 39).
eea_value.sweet_fat_salt_availability: sweet food seasonal and costly (honey); fat and salt concentrations ancestrally rare; bundled in whole-food matrix

eea_parameters.modern_default: Ultra-processed, hyperpalatable products engineered to the 'bliss point' - the mathematically optimized concentration of sugar, fat, and salt that maximizes craving - stripped of fiber and whole-food bulk. These foods decouple palatability from nutritional value and deliver calories faster than satiety signaling can register them, so the evolved fullness/reward proxies no longer track intake. Ultra-processed hyperpalatability is the modern proxy that defeats satiety.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Industrial formulation deliberately separates the reward cues (sweet/fat/salt) from the satiety cues (fiber, bulk, slow digestion) the two were ancestrally bundled together, so modern hyperpalatable food drives consumption past the point the body would otherwise stop, defeating the honest-signal logic of appetite regulation.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Satiety-honesty of food (does palatability track nutritional/caloric load?), not calorie count alone: the failure is the engineered decoupling of reward from fullness, not merely high energy density.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade: argued, not yet tested. Journalism from industry documents and interviews records that food companies tune sugar, fat and salt to a 'bliss point' that maximizes craving (Moss 2013, ext 75, 76, 439, 440); those sources do not test whether this defeats satiety. In a two-week inpatient crossover trial, 20 adults ate 508 kcal a day more on an ultra-processed diet than on an unprocessed one matched for presented calories, sugar, sodium and fiber (Hall et al. 2019, ext 866). In a review of 185 prospective studies and 58 trials, the trials found lower bodyweight, systolic blood pressure and total cholesterol with more dietary fibre, and in the prospective studies the highest fibre intakes went with 15 to 30 percent less death from all causes and from cardiovascular disease, with the benefit greatest at 25 to 29 g a day and the dose-response curves pointing to more benefit at higher intakes (Reynolds et al. 2019). The ancestral fiber figure (about 100 g a day or somewhat more against 20 g today) is a model estimate (Eaton 2006, ext 3605), which lowered the 100 to 150 g of Eaton and Konner's 1985 model (ext 39). Hadza rank honey as their favourite food, and it supplies a substantial share of their calories (Marlowe et al. 2014, ext 730).

eea_parameters.name: Multigenerational presence (older people inside the band's giving and getting)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Older people kept a place in the band's giving and getting. They gave food (ext 2063, 3088), care (ext 2084) and knowledge (ext 3827) where they could, and they were given to (ext 3088, 3665). The project's position: reciprocity runs across the whole life, so a grandmother who gave for a lifetime holds her place when she takes. What older people gave differed by group. Among the Hadza, grandmothers foraged most when their newest grandchild was youngest (ext 2063). Among the Tsimane, net food flowed down the generations: grandmothers gave a net 117 kcal a day to their grandchildren and grandfathers 223, into their 70s (ext 3088). Among the Aka, care by others, largely grandmothers, lowered mothers' work by up to 216 kcal over nine hours (ext 2084). Tsimane adults named grandparents most often as the source of the stories they knew (ext 3827). Among the Ache and Hiwi, older women did not contribute food that eased the deficits of middle-aged couples raising children, and about 10 percent of middle-aged Ache women lived with their own mothers (ext 2301). Agta adults named old age among the needs that decided whom they gave to in an experimental sharing game (ext 3665). Human longevity itself is bound up with this role: the grandmother hypothesis (and Lieberman's active-grandparent corollary) holds that the long human life after the last birth (among 52 wild mammal species, longer than chance only in humans, orcas and short-finned pilot whales, ext 3722) was selected for and made possible by older adults remaining physically active to help rear children, grandchildren, and other young kin, increasing inclusive fitness through kin-selected provisioning. Older people are thus part of the alloparental supply: a band of several generations in which the old kept a place in the exchange and were no absent generation.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Modern households are frequently bi-generational or single-generation: grandparents commonly live separately, often at a geographic distance, outside the family's daily giving and getting. In ten European countries 58 percent of grandmothers and 49 percent of grandfathers looked after a grandchild in the past year (Hank and Buber 2009, ext 4209). Where grandparents are present they are often less physically active and less part of the family's daily life than in a band of several generations.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is between older people who keep a place in the daily giving and getting of a band of several generations (M9, M3) and the modern default of grandparents who live apart from it. What they gave to the rearing of the young, in food, care and knowledge, and what was given back to them, is missing for many modern families, which thins the network of carers.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Older relatives present and inside the family's daily giving and getting: giving care, food or knowledge where they can, and being provided for. NOT mere grandparental existence or living-relative count. A surviving grandmother several time zones away does not fill the place a band of several generations gave her.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (22 Nov 2026): tested many times for what the row claims, that older people were present and inside the giving and getting. Post-reproductive survival is common across foragers (Gurven and Kaplan 2007, ext 723), and food and care from older people were measured by separate teams among the Hadza (ext 2063), the Tsimane (ext 3088) and the Aka (ext 2084); main weakness: each flow is measured in one population, and among the Ache and Hiwi older women did not ease the deficits of middle-aged couples (ext 2301). The grandmother hypothesis in the baseline is an evolutionary reading, which the label does not cover; on child survival, across 17 patrilineal populations surviving maternal grandparents went with lower child mortality and paternal grandparents did not (Strassmann and Garrard 2011, ext 3536). On child growth, among 127 Aka children grandmothers were the allomother most linked to better nutritional status, clearest from 9 months to 3 years (Meehan, Helfrecht and Quinlan 2014). On food the row states a project position (21 Nov 2026): a grandmother who gave for a lifetime need not feed anyone to hold her place. Measured flows differ by group: down the generations among the Tsimane (ext 3088); Hadza grandmothers foraged more when grandchildren were youngest (ext 2063); among the Ache and Hiwi older women did not ease the deficits of middle-aged couples (ext 2301).

evidence.author_quote: In order to elucidate the links between exercise and aging, I propose a corollary to the grandmother hypothesis, which I call the active grandparent hypothesis. According to this idea, human longevity was not only selected for but also made possible by having to work moderately during old age to help as many children, grandchildren, and other younger relatives as possible to survive and thrive. That is, while there might have been selection for genes (as yet unidentified) that help humans live past the age of fifty, there was also selection for genes that repair and maintain our bodies when we are physically active. As a result, many of the mechanisms that slow aging and extend life are turned on by physical activity, especially as we get older. Human health and longevity are thus extended both by and for physical activity.

Yet humans - like marmosets - provide a paradoxical exception to this rule.

evidence.content: Hrdy's alloparenting role in human evolution: alloparenting is particularly well developed and played a special role in the evolution of our own large-brained, slow-growing, and extraordinarily inventive species. This links the cross-species cooperative-breeding finding to the sp

evidence.content: Sear and Mace reviewed 45 populations (mostly natural-fertility populations with little or no modern medical care, historical and contemporary, across a wide geographic range) in which the effect of at least one kind of kin on child mortality had been tested. In almost all, at le

In hunter-gatherer populations with minimal or no exposure to modern medicine, about 57 percent of children survived to age 15, and the most common age of adult death was about 70 (68 to 78 across populations).

evidence.author_quote: This pattern may have evolved with mother-child food sharing, a practice that allowed aging females to enhance their daughters' fertility, thereby increasing selection against senescence
evidence.content: The grandmother hypothesis holds that long human life after menopause evolved because older women fed their weaned grandchildren, which let their daughters have babies sooner.

Across hunting records from 40 sites in subsistence societies, hunting skill rose into adulthood and peaked on average around age 33, then declined only slowly, so skill stayed high through much of adulthood.
