mechanism_ages.part: defensive output centre (periaqueductal gray)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least 460 million years, likely about 460 to 535
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first vertebrates: a periaqueductal gray homologue, the command centre for freezing, flight and defensive fighting, shared with lampreys
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Olson et al. 2017 (lamprey tract tracing, 32 animals): one lab's anatomical homology; the structure's role in lamprey defence has not been tested.
mechanism_ages.note: Dates from group T: fossil minimum 457.5 (Arandaspis), molecular 459.3 to 533.8; label follows T's suggested wording. Older figures in the A sources (haitina2007: 525 fossil, 564 molecular; Grillner lab: about 500, or over 560) are cited round numbers and are superseded by T. Defensive behaviour itself is older (invertebrates have it) but uses non-homologous circuits (ledoux2012), so it does not date the human system.

mechanism_ages.part: amygdala threat-evaluation and learning circuit
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 340 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first four-limbed vertebrates: an amygdala with the same basic plan in frogs, reptiles, birds and mammals
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Moreno and Gonzalez 2007 review of embryological, tract-tracing and neurochemical work by several labs across amniotes and frogs; amphibian functional data are thin.
mechanism_ages.note: Date from group T: crown tetrapods 337 to 351 (Wardie Shales minimum; molecular 338 to 354). Possibly older: a fish pallial region may be the amygdala homologue (portavella2004, moreno2007), which would push it to the bony-fish ancestor, group T crown osteichthyans 420.7 to 444.9 (portavella2004 says some 400 million years); that extension rests on one lab's goldfish lesions and is graded thin, so it is kept out of the label. No amygdala homologue has been identified in lamprey (suryanarayana2022), so the old field's all-vertebrates reading does not hold for this part.

mechanism_ages.part: dopamine-modulated basal ganglia circuit (action selection and outcome evaluation)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least 460 million years, likely about 460 to 535
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first vertebrates: striatum, pallidum and dopamine input with a habenula outcome-evaluation loop, shared with lampreys
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Frost-Nylen et al. 2024 and Suryanarayana et al. 2022 review lamprey tracing and physiology from essentially one lab; Yamamoto and Vernier 2011 doubt that lamprey and teleost diencephalic dopamine cells match the mammalian SNc/VTA. Weight leans toward homology on the later lamprey connectivity data.
mechanism_ages.note: Dates from group T crown vertebrates (fossil minimum 457.5, molecular 459.3 to 533.8); frostnylen2024 says about 500 million years, a cited round number. Yamamoto and Vernier place the conserved dopamine motor role at tetrapods (group T 337 to 351), which is the low end if the lamprey homology fails. This dates the general action-selection machinery that seeking runs on; it does not show reward seeking in lamprey.

mechanism_ages.part: mesolimbic reward pathway (midbrain dopamine to ventral striatum)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 165 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form's reward-specific pathway, shown in all mammals studied, with a probable counterpart in birds, reptiles and frogs
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Yamamoto and Vernier 2011: anatomical resemblance of SNc/VTA and a proposed accumbens in birds, reptiles and amphibians; the authors call mesolimbic conservation less clear, and no non-mammal reward test is in these sources.
mechanism_ages.note: Lower bound is crown mammals (Panksepp: SEEKING in all mammals), group T 164.9 to 201.5. If the bird, reptile and frog anatomy holds up as homology it would be crown tetrapods (337 to 351), which is why the row is open-ended. The tetrapod reading is probable, not shown. Lamprey striatum has no clear ventral division (suryanarayana2022). The deep circuit row above is the better public figure for the seeking system's machinery; this row records that its reward-specific wiring is less certainly that old.

mechanism_ages.part: attachment and separation distress
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 165 to 200 million years (as old as the living mammals)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first mammals: infant attachment and separation distress tied to a nursing mother, shared by the mammals tested
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Panksepp's brain stimulation work showing the separation-distress system in every mammal tested; main weakness: one programme, species not itemised, no monotreme or marsupial data, and the link to lactation is inference.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Mammalia. Panksepp E267 says at least 150 million years; Oftedal puts milk-dependent young in mammal ancestors by about 210 million years ago, so the system may be older than crown mammals. Separation calls also occur in chicks, so the behaviour alone is not mammal-only. The field value ~200Myr (mammalian) sits at the top of the crown mammal range. Group T: crown mammals 164.9 to 201.5 (fossil), 164.8 to 204.7 (molecular).

mechanism_ages.part: oxytocin and vasotocin peptides
mechanism_ages.age_label: oxytocin gene about 420 to 470 million years (as old as the jawed vertebrates); its vasotocin parent is older
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the molecular toolkit, not the bonding system: vasotocin (vasopressin) is shared with invertebrate chordate relatives; oxytocin split off from it in the first jawed vertebrates
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Theofanopoulou et al. 2021, synteny and phylogeny across 35 vertebrate genomes; main weakness: one group's reconstruction and only four invertebrate genomes.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Gnathostomata for oxytocin. These peptides were co-opted into mammalian attachment and maternal care; their age must not be printed as the age of attachment. Group T: crown gnathostomes 420.7 to 468.4. The min and max are for oxytocin only.

mechanism_ages.part: social play (rough-and-tumble)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 million years (all primates play), possibly up to about 160 to 170 million years if marsupial and placental play are one system
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human line's play system, which every living primate shares; play outside mammals evolved separately and is not part of this age
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Burghardt 2014 (all primates play in all three ways) with Iwaniuk et al. 2001 (play across 15 mammal orders); main weakness: homology is inferred from distribution only, and Burghardt et al. 2024 list a shared mammal-wide play-fighting mechanism as an open question.
mechanism_ages.note: Lower bound: crown Primates. Upper bound if marsupial and placental play prove to be one inherited system: crown Theria. Rat play fighting (Pellis E218, E223) is the best-mapped circuit; the rodent and primate common ancestor (Euarchontoglires) is a possible intermediate bound, untested. The field text "absent in reptiles" is wrong: play is documented in turtles, lizards, crocodilians, fish and invertebrates (Burghardt 2014, Dinets 2015), but as independent origins. Group T: crown primates 56 to 66 (fossil), 67.3 to 69.1 (molecular); crown therians 156.3 to 169.6 (fossil). The max is the untested upper bound, not an estimate.

mechanism_ages.part: rank detection and rank-driven brain change (social behaviour network)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 420 to 445 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first bony vertebrates: the social behaviour network that reads rank is homologous in fish, reptiles, birds and mammals
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Fernald and Maruska 2012, cichlid fish rank switching with network-wide gene activation, citing homology of the network in fish, reptiles and birds. Weakness: one lab's fish work and one review's summary of the homology; the primary comparative papers were not read.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown osteichthyans, 420.7 to 444.9 (Guiyu minimum; molecular composite 420.6 to 444.2). Clade: crown bony vertebrates (Osteichthyes: ray-finned fish plus tetrapods). Cartilaginous fish and lampreys were not covered by the source, so the circuit could be older. Serotonin-linked dominance in crayfish (Huber 1997) shows status behaviour in invertebrates, but no source claims it is the same inherited system, so it does not set the age.

mechanism_ages.part: rank-linked stress physiology, health and survival
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 25 to 34 million years in the human line; also seen in other mammal orders
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form in the primate line: rank-linked survival and stress physiology shared with baboons and macaques
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Snyder-Mackler et al. 2020, a multi-group review of long-term field studies showing status predicts survival in at least 12 species including baboons and macaques. Weakness: the species acquired social living separately several times, so the shared pattern is partly convergent and its inheritance within primates is inferred.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown catarrhines, 24.44 to 34.0. Clade for the human line: crown catarrhines (humans, apes, baboons, macaques). The pattern also appears in rabbits, meerkats, hyenas and ungulates, through several separate transitions to social living, so a single mammal-wide age would overstate homology. Sapolsky 2004 and 2005 (Cor works 91, 92) cover primate rank and health but were not reread here.

mechanism_ages.part: passivity default under prolonged uncontrollable stress (dorsal raphe serotonin)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 to 90 million years; about 165 to 200 million years if all mammals share it, as the authors say
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit as tested: shown in rats, mice and dogs and described by the authors as the default mammalian reaction
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Maier and Seligman 2016, rat dorsal raphe experiments showing passivity is the default and control is learned. Weakness: one group's rat work; "mammalian" is a generalisation, and older origins (a serotonin-linked stress state in flies) are untested for homology.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: the tested species (rats, mice, dogs) share an ancestor inside crown placentals; group T has no node for that ancestor (Boreoeutheria), so the floor uses the crown placental fossil minimum 61.6 and molecular 87.9 to 90.4 (contested between fossil and molecular readings). The authors' "mammalian" would mean crown mammals, 164.9 to 201.5. contested is set true for the dating, not the default itself. Minimum clade: the common ancestor of rodents and dogs (Boreoeutheria) as the tested species; the authors say mammalian, which would mean crown mammals. Serotonin is very old and flies show a stress-induced, serotonin-modulated inactivity state (Ries 2017), so the default may be much older, but no source tests homology.

mechanism_ages.part: prefrontal controllability detector (prelimbic, ventromedial prefrontal cortex)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 to 90 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the common ancestor of rodents and primates: the medial (agranular) prefrontal cortex that detects control in rats is homologous to the primate anterior cingulate region
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Maier and Seligman 2016 for the rat prelimbic detector, plus Laubach et al. 2018 for rodent to primate medial frontal homology. Weakness: the detector is one group's rat result, human evidence is a few imaging studies, and area-by-area homology is debated.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: the rodent and primate ancestor (Euarchontoglires) lies inside crown placentals and is not a group T node; floor from the crown placental fossil minimum 61.6, upper from the crown placental molecular range 87.9 to 90.4 (fossil and molecular readings disagree, hence contested). Clade: Euarchontoglires (rodents plus primates). No source read covers medial prefrontal cortex in other mammals, so it may be older. The granular lateral prefrontal cortex is primate-specific and is not the detector.

mechanism_ages.part: the human clock-gene system (CLOCK and BMAL1 with PERIOD and CRYPTOCHROME)
mechanism_ages.age_label: more than 500 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic clock-gene loop in the common ancestor of insects and vertebrates (bilaterian animals); its CLOCK, CYCLE/BMAL1 and cryptochrome parts reach back to the ancestor shared with sea anemones
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Rosbash 2009 summarises clock-gene orthology between flies and mammals found by many groups; the 500 million year figure is a cited lower bound for the insect-mammal split.
mechanism_ages.note: Label keeps Rosbash's sourced lower bound. Group T crown bilaterians: fossil 550.25 to 636.1 (minimum rests on Kimberella, disputed), molecular 595.7 to 688.3; if the main session prefers T, about 550 to 690 million years, contested at the minimum. Extension to the cnidarian-bilaterian ancestor (no group T node; it lies between crown animals, 550 to 833, and crown bilaterians) rests on one lab's sea anemone study and lacks Period, so it is kept out of the label (thin). The SCN as master clock is a vertebrate/mammalian arrangement and is not dated here (see unsourced).

mechanism_ages.part: daily clocks as a kind of system (cyanobacteria)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 1 to 3.5 billion years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the oldest known daily clocks, in cyanobacteria; a separate invention that is not the ancestor of the human clock
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Dvornyk et al. 2003: one molecular-clock study; the full three-gene clock dates to about 1,000 million years, older parts (kaiB, kaiC) to 2,320 to 3,800 million years, with few kaiA sequences and two calibration points.
mechanism_ages.note: The old field (about 3 billion years, cyanobacteria onward) implied the human clock descends from the cyanobacterial one. It does not: the clock proteins are unrelated and the two systems arose separately (rosbash2009). Even the cyanobacterial three-gene clock is dated to about 1 billion years; 3.5 billion is the age of kaiB/kaiC parts, which alone are not shown to keep daily time. Keep this row off the human-system headline.

mechanism_ages.part: innate immunity and inflammatory signalling (pattern-recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 550 to 830 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic system in the first animals: pattern-recognition receptors are found throughout the animal kingdom
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Flajnik and Kasahara 2010, a review of comparative immune genomics. Weakness: the animal-wide claim is one sentence citing others, and the date of the animal common ancestor rests on molecular clocks with a wide range.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown animals, fossil 550.25 to 833 (contested at the minimum, which rests on reading Kimberella as a bilaterian) and molecular 649.8 to 833.5. Clade: crown animals (Metazoa). "All multicellular" is wrong as homology: plants have their own expanded receptor families, and plants and fungi became multicellular separately. Brennan and Gilmore 2018 (Mol Biol Evol, Toll-like receptor origins) could tighten this but its OA copy sits behind a bot check and was not read.

mechanism_ages.part: adaptive immunity (RAG-based antibodies, T cell receptors, MHC)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 420 to 470 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic system in the first jawed vertebrates (shared with sharks and rays)
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Flajnik and Kasahara 2010, summarising RAG, antibody, T cell receptor and MHC genes found in every jawed vertebrate class and absent in jawless fish. Weakness: the source gives only a round 500 million years; the fossil-calibrated date must come from group T.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown gnathostomes, 420.7 to 468.4 (Guiyu minimum; molecular composite 432.1 to 468.1). The source's round "500 million years" is a little older than this range; the fossil-calibrated range is used. Clade: crown jawed vertebrates (Gnathostomata); the source says the system has been "remarkably uniform over 500 million years"; take the fossil-calibrated range from group T. Lampreys and hagfish evolved a separate adaptive system (VLRs), so it is convergent and does not extend the human system's age; B-like and T-like lymphocyte lineages may predate the jawed and jawless split. Grade replicated holds only if that date is fossil-calibrated.

mechanism_ages.part: maternal care circuitry
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 165 to 200 million years (as old as the living mammals)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first mammals: maternal care built around nursing (medial preoptic area, oxytocin, prolactin, dopamine), found in all living mammals
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Rilling and Young 2014, a review of rodent circuit work with human parallels; main weakness: the circuit is shown in rodents and humans only, and its presence in all mammals is inferred from lactation (Oftedal 2012, abstract).
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Mammalia. Oftedal dates milk-dependent young to about 210 million years ago in mammal ancestors (inference). The preoptic area also controls parental care in other vertebrates, so parts of the circuit may be older; not sourced here. Group T: crown mammals 164.9 to 201.5 (fossil).

mechanism_ages.part: human cooperative breeding (alloparenting)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 2 million years (theory)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: routine care and provisioning of young by helpers other than the mother, unique among apes and evolved separately from cooperatively breeding monkeys
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Burkart et al. 2014, one standardised test across 15 primate species, plus Burkart et al. 2025 placing the setting in early Homo about 2 million years ago; main weakness: the onset is inferred from life-history models and fossil ecology, never observed.
mechanism_ages.note: Burkart et al. 2025 argue cooperative breeding came before large brains and that weaning age fell already in australopithecines, so the true onset may be older than 2 million years. Competing scenarios (altriciality first, diet first) would put it later. Hrdy 2009 (Cor work 10) and Kramer 2010 (Cor work 193) are the standard sources but no extraction was read here. The max of 10 is only the bound set by the human-chimpanzee split (group T: 6.5 to 10, contested), not an estimate of onset.

mechanism_ages.part: the human form: a body that depends on high daily aerobic activity
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 2 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: the shift to hunting and gathering, which made high daily aerobic activity normal and, on this argument, made health upkeep depend on it
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Raichlen and Alexander 2017 model paper: the two million year activity shift comes from cited fossil and archaeological work; the link to today's dependence on exercise is argued, not tested. Raichlen et al. 2012 (humans, dogs, ferrets) supports a running-linked reward but is one small study.
mechanism_ages.note: The source says around two million years. Group T has no genus Homo node; its notes carry the same about 2 million year genus figure from Eaton and Konner 1985 (E38, verified only from the preview paragraph). The old field (about 500 million years) has no source behind it: nothing found dates movement as a zeitgeber, anti-inflammatory or mood regulator across vertebrates (see unsourced).

mechanism_ages.part: reciprocal exchange and alliances in primates
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 25 to 34 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic behaviour in the common ancestor of humans, apes and Old World monkeys: reciprocal exchange seen in chimpanzees, baboons and macaques
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Schino and Aureli 2008, a meta-analysis of grooming reciprocation in 48 groups of 22 primate species. Weakness: behavioural correlation only; homology is inferred from distribution, and similar exchanges in coatis show the trait can arise separately.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown catarrhines, 24.44 to 34.0. Clade: crown catarrhines (Cosmides and Tooby name macaques and baboons; Schino and Aureli sample is dominated by macaques). Schino and Aureli call the pattern widespread across the primate order, which could push it older, but the species list was not read. Cosmides and Tooby give "at least" the human and chimpanzee ancestor, 5 to 10 million years in 1992 estimates, as a floor, and point further back to macaques and baboons.

mechanism_ages.part: third-party norm enforcement and large-scale reciprocity (human form)
mechanism_ages.age_label: younger than the human and chimpanzee split, about 7 to 10 million years ago; exact age unknown
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: punishing violators on behalf of others, absent in chimpanzees in the one experiment that tested it
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Riedl et al. 2012, an experiment finding no third-party punishment in chimpanzees. Weakness: one study in one species read as abstract only; no source dates when in the human line this arose.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: upper bound from group T human vs chimpanzee, fossil 6.5 to 10 (contested), molecular 7 to 13. Upper bound: the human and chimpanzee common ancestor. No lower bound sourced; Tomasello et al. 2012 (Curr Anthropol, interdependence hypothesis) proposes Homo-era steps but its OA copies sit behind a bot check and were not read. Boehm (Cor works 9, 177) and Tomasello (work 14) are in Cor but were not reread.

mechanism_ages.part: pathogen and parasite avoidance behaviour (as a kind of behaviour)
mechanism_ages.age_label: found across the animal kingdom; no single age, since no source shows it is one inherited system
mechanism_ages.dates_what: a kind of behaviour found from nematodes and insects to fish, birds and mammals; no source shows it is one inherited system
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Sarabian, Curtis and McMullan 2018, a cross-species overview with experiments in nematodes, bees and bonobos. Weakness: it documents breadth, not homology, and expects commonalities because every organism faces parasites.
mechanism_ages.note: The presence of the behaviour across animals is well documented; any single date for it would treat convergent solutions as one inherited system. No source traces a shared avoidance circuit between nematodes, insects and vertebrates.

mechanism_ages.part: contamination avoidance in primates (precursor of human pathogen disgust)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 25 to 34 million years, if the primate response is the same system
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic response in the common ancestor of humans, apes and Old World monkeys: avoidance of faeces-contaminated food in bonobos, chimpanzees, macaques and mandrills
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: bonobo and macaque contamination experiments summarised in Sarabian et al. 2018. Weakness: mostly one research group and few species; continuity with human disgust is argued, not tested.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown catarrhines, 24.44 to 34.0. Clade: crown catarrhines. The human disgust expression, its sexual domain and its moral extension have no dated source here: Curtis et al. 2011 show disgust is universal in humans, which makes it old within our species but does not date it. Moral disgust is human-only by definition and its age is unsourced.

mechanism_ages.part: brain appetite brake (leptin and melanocortin MC4 signalling that cut food intake)
mechanism_ages.age_label: more than 420 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first jawed vertebrates: leptin and brain melanocortin receptors that reduce food intake, shown in bony fish and mammals but not in lamprey brains
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Deck et al. 2017 review: injected leptin cut food intake in five fish species across several groups, as in mammals; fish leptin sequences differ a lot from mammalian leptin, and the lamprey evidence (Haitina et al. 2007) is one lab's.
mechanism_ages.note: Group T: crown osteichthyans 420.7 to 444.9 (the minimum, from the fish feeding experiments) and crown gnathostomes 420.7 to 468.4 (likely origin on Haitina's reading, since sharks express brain melanocortin receptors). It should be younger than crown vertebrates (460 to 535), since lamprey melanocortin receptors are not in the brain. Leptin as a fat-store signal is not shown in fish (deck2017 ext 1) and was not dated; the old field's 500 million years is too old for the brain appetite brake.

mechanism_ages.part: the human form: a larger daily energy budget and more body fat than other apes
mechanism_ages.age_label: less than about 6.5 to 10 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: faster metabolism and greater fat stores that evolved in the human line after it split from chimpanzees and bonobos
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Pontzer et al. 2016 (doubly labelled water, 141 humans, 56 apes): one study, zoo and sanctuary apes, small ape samples.
mechanism_ages.note: Pontzer shows the change happened in the human line but does not date it within that line; the upper limit is the human-chimpanzee split, group T fossil 6.5 to 10 (contested; molecular 7 to 13). Pontzer's constrained-energy finding (Cor work 61) is a within-lifetime adjustment measured in living adults and supports no age.

mechanism_ages.part: sexual desire: hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least 460 million years, likely about 460 to 535 (as old as the vertebrates)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic hormonal circuit in the first vertebrates: GnRH from the hypothalamus driving the pituitary and gonads, already present in lampreys
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Sower et al. 2012, lamprey GnRH peptides and receptors from a long lab programme; main weakness: one group's review, and its 550 million year lineage figure is not a calibrated node date.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Vertebrata (lamprey plus jawed vertebrates). Sower gives over 550 million years for the agnathan lineage. This dates the hormonal axis; the brain circuits of desire (preoptic area, ventromedial hypothalamus) are not dated by a source read here. The field value ~500Myr sexual is about right for the axis. Group T: crown vertebrates at least 457.5 (fossil, soft max 636.1), molecular 459.3 to 533.8; wording follows T's suggestion.

mechanism_ages.part: human pair bonding
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 2 to 4 million years (contested)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: the hominin pair bond, evolved in the human line after the split from chimpanzees; it is not inherited from early mammals, where social monogamy arose about 60 separate times
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest sources: Reno et al. 2003 (A. afarensis dimorphism like modern humans, placing the pair bond about 4 million years ago) against Gordon et al. 2008 (gorilla-like dimorphism, so later, with reduced dimorphism by early Homo about 2 million years ago); main weakness: mating systems are inferred from fossil body-size dimorphism, which Plavcan 2012 and Schacht and Kramer 2019 call unreliable.
mechanism_ages.note: The early side (about 4 million years, australopithecines) rests on Reno et al.; Lovejoy 2009 on Ardipithecus, named in the dispatch, was not read in full and is not used; the late side (early Homo, about 2 million years) on Gordon et al. and the reduced dimorphism in early Homo. Weight leans slightly to the later date: Schacht and Kramer report a general consensus that dimorphism was greater in the past and fell over time, and they cite several analyses that find A. afarensis strongly dimorphic (Lockwood et al. 1996 and 2007, Gordon et al. 2008); neither side is decisive. Fisher E193 (3.2 million years, Lucy) sits inside the range and is a trade-book theoretical claim. Hard outer bound: the human-chimpanzee split (group T: 6.5 to 10, fossil, contested).

mechanism_ages.part: C-tactile (CT) touch afferents
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 million years, probably under 90 (placental mammals)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic nerve channel as shown so far: slow unmyelinated touch fibres in hairy skin recorded in humans, monkeys, cats and rodents, so present in their common placental ancestor
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: single-fibre recordings by several groups in cats, monkeys and humans (reviewed by Liljencrantz and Olausson 2014), with a molecular rodent counterpart (Vrontou et al. 2013); main weakness: few placental species, no marsupial or monotreme data, and homology rests on similar response properties.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Boreoeutheria (common ancestor of primates, rodents and cats). The field value ~200Myr (mammalian) assumes all mammals have CTs; that is not shown. If CTs are found in marsupials or monotremes the age rises to crown Theria or crown Mammalia. Grooming and allogrooming are not dated by any source read here. Group T has no node for the primate-rodent-carnivore ancestor (Boreoeutheria). It contains crown primates, so it is older than 56 (T crown primates fossil minimum), and it is younger than crown placentals (T: 61.6 to 164.6 fossil, 87.9 to 90.4 molecular). The max is the crown placental soft maximum, not an estimate.

challenges_set_aside.title: Depression as sickness behavior? A test of the host defense hypothesis in a high pathogen population (Tsimane)
challenges_set_aside.reason: Refiled as support. The scores show low mood firing on its own triggers, here immune activation, in a forager-horticulturalist population, which is what OF2 predicts. One population with no matched comparison cannot score falsifier 1.

challenges_set_aside.title: Functional disability and social conflict increase risk of depression in older adulthood among Bolivian forager-farmers (Tsimane), prevalence finding
challenges_set_aside.reason: Set aside as a weak test and moved out of the core set. It is one cross-sectional sample, and its comparison with industrial prevalence runs across questionnaires that are not equivalent. The study's correlates (disability, a lost provider role, conflict) stay in the atlas.

changed.old: Specific physiological and behavioral systems calibrate during specific developmental windows to environmental inputs within evolved parameters; inputs outside those parameters produce persistent miscalibration - established independently by Bowlby's attachment developmental calibration, McEwen's HPA-axis calibration neuroendocrinology, and Felitti's ACE Study dose-response evidence for durable effects of early-life exposure. The ACE leg is an association from adults' own recall. For psychiatric outcomes about half of it is carried by genes and family and part stays. For early death no design that controls for genes or family has tested it.
changed.new: Specific physiological and behavioral systems calibrate during specific developmental windows to environmental inputs within evolved parameters; inputs far outside those parameters leave a lasting mark - established independently by the Bucharest randomised trial of foster care against institutional rearing, the English and Romanian Adoptees natural experiment, and cross-fostering experiments in rats, with McEwen's HPA-axis neuroendocrinology as the bodily route. Inside the ordinary range of homes, differences in upbringing explain little of how adults differ in personality: adoptive siblings reared together correlate .04 (Plomin and Daniels 1987). Recalled childhood adversity (the ACE Study) was a leg of this convergence until 21 Nov 2026 and is withdrawn: it is a link from adults' own recall.

studies.cite: Plomin R, Daniels D (1987). Why are children in the same family so different from one another? Behavioral and Brain Sciences.
Pinquart M, Feussner C, Ahnert L (2013). Meta-analytic evidence for stability in attachments from infancy to early adulthood. Attachment & Human Development.

Baldwin JR, Wang B, Karwatowska L, Schoeler T, Tsaligopoulou A, Munafo MR, Pingault JB (2023). Childhood maltreatment and mental health problems: a systematic review and meta-analysis of quasi-experimental studies. American Journal of Psychiatry.
Danese A, Widom CS (2020). Objective and subjective experiences of child maltreatment and their relationships with psychopathology. Nature Human Behaviour.

changed.old: Chronic or developmental adverse experiences cascade across physiological systems in a dose-response manner, with effects that propagate and self-maintain across domains (metabolic, immune, neural, behavioral) - established independently by Felitti's ACE Study clinical epidemiology, McEwen's allostatic-load neuroendocrinology, and Panksepp's cross-system inhibition evidence for affective-system propagation. The ACE leg is an association from adults' own recall. For psychiatric outcomes about half of it is carried by genes and family and part stays. For early death no design that controls for genes or family has tested it.
changed.new: Chronic adverse load cascades across physiological systems, with effects that propagate and self-maintain across domains (metabolic, immune, neural, behavioral) - established independently by McEwen's allostatic-load neuroendocrinology and Panksepp's cross-system inhibition evidence for affective-system propagation. The ACE Study was a third leg, and the source of the word 'Dose-Response' in this convergence's name, until 21 Nov 2026 and is withdrawn: it is a link from adults' own recall (Danese and Widom 2020), and about half of it is carried by genes and family for psychiatric outcomes (Baldwin et al. 2023). The convergence now stands on two lines.

studies.cite: Baldwin JR, Wang B, Karwatowska L, Schoeler T, Tsaligopoulou A, Munafo MR, Pingault JB (2023). Childhood maltreatment and mental health problems: a systematic review and meta-analysis of quasi-experimental studies. American Journal of Psychiatry.

changed.old: Developmental miscalibration carried forward and chronic dysregulation displace the reading of the current input without making the output a disease: the output answers a threshold set early, or a loop that keeps running, more than the present input.
changed.new: A setting left by deprivation far outside the evolved range (DA7) and chronic dysregulation displace the reading of the current input without making the output a disease: the output answers that setting, or a loop that keeps running, more than the present input. An ordinary hard childhood is no such setting, and even maltreatment, once genes and family are adjusted for, explains little of how an adult feels (DA7).

studies.cite: Baldwin JR, Wang B, Karwatowska L, Schoeler T, Tsaligopoulou A, Munafo MR, Pingault JB (2023). Childhood maltreatment and mental health problems: a systematic review and meta-analysis of quasi-experimental studies. American Journal of Psychiatry.

changed.old: Field data from preindustrial-style foraging/horticultural societies place habitual sleep within a window in the rough range of ~6-7 hours of nocturnal sleep, but the load-bearing ancestral feature is the alignment of the sleep episode to circadian phase, not hitting a particular hour count.
changed.new: Field data from three preindustrial societies (Hadza, San, Tsimane) place habitual sleep within a window in the rough range of ~6-7 hours of nocturnal sleep; subsistence horticulturalists on Tanna, Vanuatu, slept about 7.4 to 7.9 hours (Smit et al. 2019). The ancestral feature that counts is the alignment of the sleep episode to circadian phase; the hour count differed between groups.

studies.cite: Smit AN, Broesch T, Siegel JM, Mistlberger RE (2019). Sleep timing and duration in indigenous villages with and without electric lighting on Tanna Island, Vanuatu. Scientific Reports.

changed.old: In every forager group with a record, food moved between households before it was eaten.
changed.new: In every forager group with a record, food moved between households.

studies.cite: Berbesque JC, Wood BM, Crittenden AN, Mabulla A, Marlowe FW (2016). Eat first, share later: Hadza hunter-gatherer men consume more while foraging than in central places. Evolution and Human Behavior.

changed.old: This was not a cultural add-on but species architecture: a human child requires on the order of 13 million calories from birth to independence, and humans breed faster (every 3-4 years) than other apes (every 6-8 years) while producing larger, slower-maturing babies - a life-history paradox solvable only by shared provisioning.
changed.new: This is part of human biology: a human child requires on the order of 13 million calories from birth to independence, and humans breed faster (every 3-4 years) than chimpanzees and orangutans (about every 5.5 and 7.7 years; gorillas breed about every 3.8 years, Galdikas and Wood 1990) while producing larger, slower-maturing babies - a life-history paradox solvable only by shared provisioning.

studies.cite: Galdikas BMF, Wood JW (1990). Birth spacing patterns in humans and apes. American Journal of Physical Anthropology.

changed.old: Forager women had their first child at about 19 to 20: Hadza 18.8, !Kung 19.2, Ache 19.5, Hiwi 20.5, Agta 20.2.
changed.new: Forager women had their first child at about 19 to 20 in five groups (Hadza 18.8, !Kung 19.2, Ache 19.5, Hiwi 20.5, Agta 20.2) and at about 15.4 among the Pume (Kramer 2008).

studies.cite: Kramer KL (2008). Early sexual maturity among Pume foragers of Venezuela: fitness implications of teen motherhood. American Journal of Physical Anthropology.

changed.old: Ancestrally, sleep occurred within a stable phase relationship to the solar/circadian night: onset shortly after dusk, offset near or before dawn, with the sleep episode anchored to internal circadian time.
changed.new: Ancestrally, sleep occurred within a stable phase relationship to the solar/circadian night: onset about three hours after sunset (3.3 hours on average among Hadza, San and Tsimane, Yetish et al. 2015; about three hours in rural Haiti without electricity, Knutson 2014), offset near or before dawn, with the sleep episode anchored to internal circadian time.

studies.cite: Yetish G, Kaplan H, Gurven M, Wood B, Pontzer H, Manger PR, Wilson C, McGregor R, Siegel JM (2015). Natural sleep and its seasonal variations in three pre-industrial societies. Current Biology.
Knutson KL (2014). Sleep duration, quality, and timing and their associations with age in a community without electricity in Haiti. American Journal of Human Biology.

changed.old: Human longevity itself is bound up with this role: the grandmother hypothesis (and Lieberman's active-grandparent corollary) holds that uniquely long human lifespans were selected for and made possible by older adults remaining physically active to help rear children, grandchildren, and other young kin, increasing inclusive fitness through kin-selected provisioning.
changed.new: Human longevity itself is bound up with this role: the grandmother hypothesis (and Lieberman's active-grandparent corollary) holds that the long human life after the last birth (among 52 wild mammal species, longer than chance only in humans, orcas and short-finned pilot whales, Ellis et al. 2018) was selected for and made possible by older adults remaining physically active to help rear children, grandchildren, and other young kin, increasing inclusive fitness through kin-selected provisioning.

studies.cite: Ellis S, Franks DW, Nattrass S, Cant MA, Bradley DL, Giles D, Balcomb KC, Croft DP (2018). Postreproductive lifespans are rare in mammals. Ecology and Evolution.

changed.old: (1) The family one is biologically related to is now small, geographically dispersed, and often the ONLY kin one regularly co-resides with, so the kin one has are concentrated in a tiny stable household rather than diffused through a larger chosen group.
changed.new: (1) The family one is biologically related to is now small and, for about two in three adults, not all within reach (in the US, of adults with a living parent or grown child, three in four have one within 30 miles, about a third have all of them that near, and 13 percent share a home with one; Choi et al. 2020), and often the ONLY kin one regularly co-resides with, so the kin one has are concentrated in a tiny stable household rather than diffused through a larger chosen group.

studies.cite: Choi H, Schoeni RF, Wiemers EE, Hotz VJ, Seltzer JA (2020). Spatial Distance Between Parents and Adult Children in the United States. Journal of Marriage and Family.

changed.old: Online networks reproduce the same ~5/15 inner structure when genuine ties are measured (support clique ~4, sympathy group ~14, statistically indistinguishable from offline values), and mean platform friend counts hover near ~150-180, but the bulk of nominal connections are inactive labels rather than relationships (only ~27.6% of online 'friends' are reported as genuine).
changed.new: Online networks reproduce the same ~5/15 inner structure when genuine ties are measured (support clique ~4, sympathy group ~14, statistically indistinguishable from offline values), and mean platform friend counts hover near ~150-190 (across all 721 million Facebook users of May 2011 the mean was about 190 and the median 99; Ugander et al. 2011), but the bulk of nominal connections are inactive labels rather than relationships (only ~27.6% of online 'friends' are reported as genuine).

studies.cite: Ugander J, Karrer B, Backstrom L, Marlow C (2011). The Anatomy of the Facebook Social Graph. arXiv preprint arXiv:1111.4503.

changed.old: Ancestral children typically developed in the presence of grandparents - especially post-reproductive grandmothers - who were active, provisioning members of the group.
changed.new: Older people kept a place in the band's giving and getting. They gave food (Hawkes et al. 1997, Hooper et al. 2015), care (Meehan et al. 2013) and knowledge (Schniter et al. 2018) where they could, and they were given to (Hooper et al. 2015, Smith et al. 2019). The project's position: reciprocity runs across the whole life, so a grandmother who gave for a lifetime holds her place when she takes. What older people gave differed by group. Among the Ache and Hiwi, older women did not contribute food that eased the deficits of middle-aged couples raising children, and about 10 percent of middle-aged Ache women lived with their own mothers (Hill and Hurtado 2009).

studies.cite: Hill K, Hurtado AM (2009). Cooperative breeding in South American hunter-gatherers. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

changed.old: Cortical override of subcortical activation is metabolically expensive, and chronic defensive activation downregulates the cortical override machinery itself.
changed.new: Cortical override of subcortical activation is costly and tiring, and chronic defensive activation downregulates the cortical override machinery itself.

studies.cite: Kurzban R (2010). Does the brain consume additional glucose during self-control tasks? Evolutionary Psychology.

changed.new: Part of the energy spent in activity is offset by lower basal expenditure: about 28 percent in adults living ordinary lives (Careau et al. 2021).

studies.cite: Careau V, Halsey LG, Pontzer H, Ainslie PN, Andersen LF, Anderson LJ, et al. (2021). Energy compensation and adiposity in humans. Current Biology.

changed.old: In industrial societies the link between men's status and number of children is weak, and higher-status people often have fewer children.
changed.new: In industrial societies the link between men's status and number of children is weaker than in pre-industrial societies, and the sexes differ: men with higher incomes still have more children, mainly because poor men more often stay childless, while higher income in women and more education in both sexes typically go with fewer children (Stulp and Barrett 2016).

studies.cite: Stulp G, Barrett L (2016). Wealth, fertility and adaptive behaviour in industrial populations. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

changed.old: The modern reversal is argued (Boyd 2005), not graded here.
changed.new: The modern link is tested: in industrial populations wealth, measured as income, went with higher fertility in 8 of 12 longitudinal findings, men's income went with more children and women's income and education with fewer (Stulp and Barrett 2016); the grade of this row covers the ancestral link only.

studies.cite: Stulp G, Barrett L (2016). Wealth, fertility and adaptive behaviour in industrial populations. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

changed.old: The modern side here rests on Richerson and Boyd's argument (Boyd 2005, theoretical); in three industrial samples the link between men's wealth and their number of children was the weakest of eleven human samples, though still positive (Nettle and Pollet 2008), and in Britain higher-income men had more children only because low-income men were more often childless, while women's own income went with fewer children (Nettle and Pollet 2008).
changed.new: Across industrial populations, wealth, measured as income, went with higher fertility in 8 of 12 longitudinal findings, and income went with more children in men and fewer in women (Stulp and Barrett 2016); in three industrial samples the link between men's wealth and their number of children was the weakest of eleven human samples, though still positive (Nettle and Pollet 2008), and in Britain higher-income men had more children only because low-income men were more often childless, while women's own income went with fewer children (Nettle and Pollet 2008).

studies.cite: Stulp G, Barrett L (2016). Wealth, fertility and adaptive behaviour in industrial populations. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

knocked_down.cite: David M. Buss (editor) (2016). The Handbook of Evolutionary Psychology, Volume 1: Foundations (2nd ed.).
knocked_down.content: According to the strategic pluralism model of mating, women evolved to make trade-offs between two sets of attributes when evaluating men as potential mates: men's degree of health/viability ('good genes') and their level of commitment/investment in the relationship and subsequent offspring. The ovulatory shift hypothesis predicts and confirms that women's mate preferences vary across the reproductive cycle in very specific and theoretically consistent ways - including preference for more symmetrical men as short-term mates specifically during high-fertility windows.
knocked_down.note: in a preregistered study of 157 women across two cycles confirmed by hormone tests, preferences for men's behaviour did not shift with fertility (Stern et al. 2020), and in 584 women tested repeatedly, preferences for masculine faces did not track their hormone levels (Jones et al. 2018).

tests.cite: Stern J, Gerlach TM, Penke L (2020). Probing Ovulatory-Cycle Shifts in Women's Preferences for Men's Behaviors. Psychological Science.

Jones BC, Hahn AC, Fisher CI, Wang H, Kandrik M, Han C, Fasolt V, Morrison D, Lee AJ, Holzleitner IJ, O'Shea KJ, Roberts SC, Little AC, DeBruine LM (2018). No Compelling Evidence that Preferences for Facial Masculinity Track Changes in Women's Hormonal Status. Psychological Science.

knocked_down.cite: Curtis V, de Barra M, Aunger R (2011). Disgust as an Adaptive System for Disease Avoidance Behaviour. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.
knocked_down.content: Disgust sensitivity is adaptively calibrated to current physiological vulnerability. Women show increased disgust during the first trimester of pregnancy when the immune system is suppressed to tolerate paternal genetic material in the blastocyst. Salivary progesterone correlates positively with disgust sensitivity in normally cycling women - progesterone being the endocrine cue for immune downregulation. Opiate users, whose immune systems are pharmacologically suppressed, make fewer errors identifying disgust faces. Conversely, hunger downregulates disgust for food specifically while maintaining disgust for other pathogen cues - 15 hours of food deprivation reduced facial expressions of disgust to food but not to body wastes.
knocked_down.note: in 375 women tested weekly, changes in progesterone did not track changes in disgust (Jones et al. 2018).

tests.cite: Jones BC, Hahn AC, Fisher CI, Wang H, Kandrik M, Lee AJ, Tybur JM, DeBruine LM (2018). Hormonal correlates of pathogen disgust: testing the compensatory prophylaxis hypothesis. Evolution and Human Behavior.

knocked_down.cite: Fisher, Helen (2016). Anatomy of Love: A Natural History of Mating, Marriage, and Why We Stray.
knocked_down.content: In the 'sweaty T-shirt' experiment, women sniffed the T-shirts of anonymous men and selected the T-shirts of those they felt were the sexiest. They selected the T-shirts of men with genes that were different from their own in a specific region of the immune system - the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). Fisher proposes that these women were unconsciously attracted to men with different MHC genes because similarity between partners in this part of the immune system can lead to complications of fertility and pregnancy. In a subsequent investigation, women married to men who shared similar genes in this part of the immune system were also more adulterous. The more of these genes a woman shared with her spouse, the more extra partners she engaged.
knocked_down.note: a meta-analysis of 30 studies in seven primate species, humans included, found no tendency to choose MHC-dissimilar mates (Winternitz et al. 2017), and among 3,691 married couples MHC similarity was no different from random pairings (Croy et al. 2020).

tests.cite: Winternitz J, Abbate JL, Huchard E, Havlicek J, Garamszegi LZ (2017). Patterns of MHC-dependent mate selection in humans and nonhuman primates: a meta-analysis. Molecular Ecology.

Croy I, Ritschel G, Kressner-Kiel D, Schaefer L, Hummel T, Havlicek J, Sauter J, Ehninger G, Schmidt AH (2020). Marriage does not relate to major histocompatibility complex: a genetic analysis based on 3691 couples. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences.

knocked_down.cite: Robert M. Sapolsky (2017). Behave: The Biology of Humans at Our Best and Worst.
knocked_down.content: By the 1970s the dogma held that subordinate organisms are the most stressed and unhealthy, a rule the book says turned out to depend on the kind of hierarchy. Lab rodents, primates from rhesus monkeys to lemurs, hamsters, guinea pigs, wolves, rabbits, pigs, fish, and sugar gliders all show that subordinate individuals have elevated resting glucocorticoids - chronic activation of the stress response even in the absence of acute stressors. The worst stress-related health in humans typically occurs in middle management, with its killer combination of high work demands but little autonomy - responsibility without control.

knocked_down.cite: Clubb R, Mason G (2003). Captivity effects on wide-ranging carnivores. Nature.
knocked_down.content: In their comparison of caged carnivores (order Carnivora), Clubb and Mason report that natural home-range size predicted infant mortality in captivity, measured as deaths as a share of births (median home range F1,21 = 6.04, P = 0.012; minimum home range F1,19 = 12.60, P = 0.001), also with body weight controlled. Wild and captive infant mortality rates did not covary (F1,6 = 0.08), and infant mortality in the wild was unrelated to range size. The same group could not repeat the infant mortality result with an enlarged dataset in 2016.

knocked_down.cite: Clubb R, Mason GJ (2007). Natural behavioural biology as a risk factor in carnivore welfare: How analysing species differences could help zoos improve enclosures. Applied Animal Behaviour Science.

weaker.cite: Marmot, Michael (2004). The Status Syndrome: How Social Standing Affects Our Health and Longevity.
weaker.content: People at the same level in the occupational hierarchy with differing amounts of control had markedly different rates of disease - low control consistently led to more disease. weaker.note: a meta-analysis of 25 cohort studies and one case-control study found a pooled relative risk of ischaemic heart disease of 1.10 for low job control, mostly rated by the workers themselves, and 1.06 for job strain where exposure was measured by job-exposure matrix, and its authors judge that small effects, heterogeneity and bias of unknown direction preclude a causal reading (Bonde et al. 2026).

weaker.cite: Eisenberger NI, Lieberman MD, Williams KD (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science.
weaker.content: In an fMRI study of a virtual ball-tossing game, the anterior cingulate cortex was more active when participants were excluded than when they were included, and its activity tracked their reported distress, a pattern the authors read as paralleling physical pain studies.
weaker.note: the largest meta-analysis of Cyberball fMRI (Mwilambwe-Tshilobo and Spreng 2021, 53 studies, 1,817 people) found reliable activation in the ventral anterior cingulate and none in the dorsal part, even at a lowered threshold. A meta-analysis of 46 articles that reported anterior cingulate activity (Rotge et al. 2015) found both parts active, and tied the distress participants rated more specifically to the ventral parts; it took only studies that reported anterior cingulate activity, so it cannot test whether the dorsal part is reliably active. Exclusion activity in the anterior cingulate holds in its ventral part; the dorsal site where the 2003 study placed it did not hold in the larger test.

rows.title: Environmental enrichment reduces cocaine seeking and reinstatement induced by cues and stress but not by cocaine
rows.reason: Filed against DC3. The sentence of Cor: "The drug then changes the body in its own right: tolerance, withdrawal, and wanting set off by the places and people of use (Koob and Le Moal 2001, Volkow et al. 2016, Robinson and Berridge 1993, Henningfield and Keenan 1993)." Seeking set off by the drug itself is the body's change, which Cor states. The cue and stress halves of the same study support Cor. Where no defect is the cause, the drug gets replaced by the real thing, such as people who need you and give back. The real thing is hard to build under the influence, so the drug comes down while the real thing comes in. Tapering is not a rule for every medication: where stopping suddenly is biologically dangerous, as with certain drugs and with alcohol, never stop suddenly, and do it with a doctor. Where a defect is the cause, the drug may be treating a disease. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Letter of response to Nabi Z, Stansfeld J, Plöderl M, Wood L, Moncrieff J. Effects of lithium on suicide and suicidal behaviour: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials. Epidemiol Psychiatr Sci. 2022 Sep 16;31:e65. doi: 10.1017/S204579602200049X
rows.reason: Filed against another finding in the atlas (Nabi et al. 2022), which reads: "Assumes no suicides in trials that did not report them (one trial); counts Katz 2022 as 1 against 1 suicide, which Bschor 2022 disputes." An argument with no data of its own, so it counts neither for nor against Cor. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Is there a lithium withdrawal syndrome? An examination of the evidence
rows.reason: A narrative review counts only for data it reports and the abstract reports none, while the pooled and rapid-against-gradual studies Cor holds (Suppes et al. 1991, Faedda et al. 1993, Baldessarini et al. 1996) found an early excess after stopping. Where no defect is the cause, the drug gets replaced by the real thing, such as people who need you and give back. The real thing is hard to build under the influence, so the drug comes down while the real thing comes in. Tapering is not a rule for every medication: where stopping suddenly is biologically dangerous, as with certain drugs and with alcohol, never stop suddenly, and do it with a doctor. Where a defect is the cause, the drug may be treating a disease. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Loss of dopamine transporters in methamphetamine abusers recovers with protracted abstinence
rows.reason: Relapse was assumed from dropping out and not measured, heavier earlier use could explain both the low scan and the dropout, and nothing about what they came back to was measured. Twelve people do not outweigh the larger follow-ups behind DC3's sentence that the body's change does not decide whether a habit lasts (Robins et al. 1974, 943 men back from Vietnam; Maddux and Desmond 1982, 248 users in San Antonio). The five of these twelve who stayed off the drug are the record behind DC3's sentence that the change comes down. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: The rearing environment and risk for major depression: a Swedish national high-risk home-reared and adopted-away co-sibling control study (2 records)
rows.reason: Siblings adopted away from a parent diagnosed with depression were diagnosed with it 19 to 23 percent less often than their home-reared siblings, from a home they also lived in through adolescence; DA7 states this itself as a modest effect on a registered diagnosis. In a subgroup the cut vanished when an adoptive parent or stepsibling had a depression diagnosis or the adoptive home broke up through a death or a divorce before age 15. The design cannot tell a home that matters while the person lives in it from a lasting early effect, so the subgroup result counts neither way, and one register study is not as strong as the twin meta-analysis behind DA7's sentence (Polderman et al. 2015). It stays in the atlas.

set_aside_groups.label: The study measured something else
set_aside_groups.summary: Set beside the sentence of Cor it was filed against, the study measured a different thing: another outcome, another exposure, another kind of society, or a comparison between two points inside modern life, where Cor measures modern life against how humans lived.

rows.title: Depression as sickness behavior? A test of the host defense hypothesis in a high pathogen population (Tsimane)
rows.reason: Refiled as support. The scores show low mood firing on its own triggers, here immune activation, in a forager-horticulturalist population, which is what OF2 predicts. With one population and no matched comparison, it cannot show whether depression, low mood that finds no answer and stays, is rarer there than in industrial societies. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Functional disability and social conflict increase risk of depression in older adulthood among Bolivian forager-farmers (Tsimane), prevalence finding
rows.reason: It measured, at one time, how many older Tsimane adults regularly report depressive symptoms on a questionnaire. Low mood is the signal and fires in every human population; depression is low mood that finds no answer and stays, which a one-time symptom score does not measure. The comparison with industrial prevalence is the authors', across questionnaires that are not equivalent. The study's correlates (disability, a lost provider role, conflict) stay in the atlas.

rows.title: Psychotropic substance-seeking: evolutionary pathology or adaptation? (3 records)
rows.reason: Cor's hijack claim covers a drug that is purified, fast or supplied without limit (DA4). This record is about plant drugs at plant strength, which Cor holds to be old and no hijack. The authors apply the mismatch account to purified and synthetic drugs themselves.

rows.reason: Cor's hijack claim covers a drug that is purified, fast or supplied without limit (DA4). This record is about plant drugs at plant strength, which Cor holds to be old and no hijack. The authors grant that heroin may be a real mismatch.

rows.title: Addiction as a brain disease revised: why it still matters, and the need for consilience (the record on chimpanzees in withdrawal choosing morphine)
rows.reason: It describes the change a drug makes in the body, which Cor states itself: a substance effect is a physical cause (OF2), and it does not decide whether a habit lasts (DC3). It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Addiction as a brain disease revised: why it still matters, and the need for consilience (the record on rats giving up the drug for a sweet alternative)
rows.reason: It shows that a competing reward ends drug taking in rats and in paid programmes; that is no test of what a person comes back to (DC3). It stays in the atlas.

rows.reason: It measured how much adolescents used social media, and the hours on a feed are not Cor's measure: a feed is a stand-in, and what is missing does the harm (DA4). It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: The associations of active and passive social media use with well-being: A critical scoping review
rows.reason: It measured active and passive use of social media, and how much or which way a person uses a feed is not Cor's measure: a feed is a stand-in, and what is missing does the harm (DA4). It stays in the atlas.

rows.reason: It describes one settled village and gives no count; Cor's row on who lived in a camp is about mobile forager camps and rests on a census of 32 societies. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Infant allocare in traditional societies
rows.reason: It measured how much hands-on care others gave within two groups; Cor's sentence is about shared food for the young as a condition of the species. It found the saving of mothers' time that Cor's row describes. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Norm violations and punishments across human societies

rows.title: Risk and reciprocity in Meriam food sharing
rows.reason: It measured whether food shares between households were paid back in a settled island community; Cor's sentences are about gossip, ridicule and exclusion in mobile bands. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Resilience to Major Life Stressors Is Not as Common as Thought
rows.reason: It measured life satisfaction after losing a spouse, a marriage or a job; the sentence of Cor it was filed against is about PTSD after a frightening event. A lasting drop where the loss is not replaced fits Cor's reading of grief (M3). It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Questioning an axiom: better prognosis for schizophrenia in the developing world?
rows.reason: It was filed against Cor's record of the WHO re-analysis (Hopper and Wanderling 2000). That record names this review: a tabulation of 23 studies in low and middle income countries with no comparison group from high income countries, so it does not test the contrast the WHO record reports. 'Developing country' is a form: neither the WHO comparison nor this review measured what people had around them, so neither counts for or against the mismatch reading. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Comparison between an African town and a neighbouring village shows delayed, but not decreased, sleep during the early stages of urbanisation
rows.reason: A farming village with hard labour, bad beds and crowded rooms is not how humans lived either, so the comparison sets one mismatch against another and does not test light at night. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Human social organization during the Late Pleistocene: Beyond the nomadic-egalitarian model
rows.reason: The data it reports are mostly sedentary Holocene societies with stored or aquatic foods, which is not the mobile-forager baseline Cor's row describes, and its Pleistocene claim rests on indirect archaeological signs. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: The impact of pretend play on children's development: A review of the evidence
rows.reason: The causal tests it reviews are mostly adult-led play training in preschools, which is the adult-structured form Cor's row excludes, so it did not measure self-organised mixed-age play. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Influence of housing conditions on the acquisition of intravenous heroin and cocaine self-administration in rats
rows.reason: It measured something else: intravenous drug taking with no choice and ordinary cage groups in place of a colony, and its early heroin result goes the same way as Rat Park. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Questioning an axiom: better prognosis for schizophrenia in the developing world?

The review gives no death rates for developed against developing centres, so it does not reverse the WHO comparison either (Hopper and Wanderling 2000). It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: The pituri story: a review of the historical literature surrounding traditional Australian Aboriginal use of nicotine in Central Australia

rows.title: Socioeconomic status modifies heritability of IQ in young children
rows.reason: It measured IQ in 7-year-olds still living in that home, not how adults feel, and a larger meta-analysis found the pattern only in the US (Tucker-Drob and Bates 2016). It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: The psychophysiology of posttraumatic stress disorder: a meta-analysis

rows.title: Partisan Intoxication or Policy Voting?
rows.reason: Filed against EEA-SOC-19. The sentence of Cor: "Large labelled groups (parties, nations, teams) supply alliance cues without any shared life." Why people vote as they do is another question from whether party labels supply alliance cues and feelings of 'us and them', which is what Cor's sentence and its polarisation figures are about. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: A bidirectional model of sleep and technology use: A theoretical review of How much, for whom, and which mechanisms
rows.reason: Filed against M7. The sentence of Cor: "The mismatch lies in timing more than in sleep duration." Cor's claim is about the clock (melatonin and phase), and on that the review agrees with Cor. Minutes to fall asleep is another measure. The review also notes that daylight earlier in the day lessens the effect, which is Cor's other half. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Effects of Housing First approaches on health and well-being of adults who are homeless or at risk of homelessness: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
rows.reason: Filed against DC3. The sentence of Cor: "What the person comes back to decides (project position): people who know and need them, and a role among them (EEA-SOC-01, EEA-SOC-11)." Whether the flat brought what Cor's baseline rows name (people who know and need the person, a role, giving and getting back) was not measured, so the study does not test this sentence. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Large-scale cooperation in small-scale foraging societies
rows.reason: Filed against M11. The sentence of Cor: "Beyond that ceiling, cooperation requires institutional scaffolding (formal rules, third-party enforcement, shared fictions) rather than direct reciprocity." The records count people in communal hunts; they do not show that cooperation at that scale ran without shared norms, rules or enforcement, which is what Cor's sentence is about. Cor's M11 gradient already counts norm-scaffolded cooperation beyond 150 as resolution by other means. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Specific 50-kHz vocalizations are tightly linked to particular types of behavior in juvenile rats anticipating play
rows.reason: Filed against another finding in the atlas (Panksepp 2011), which reads: "Rats produce 50-kHz ultrasonic chirps during play that are homologous to human laughter." The study measured which movements the calls go with, not whether the state behind them is positive; the authors' own reading in the atlas's other record of the same recordings is that the calls communicate positive mood. Calls that coordinate play and calls that mark a positive state can both be true, as with human laughter. It stays in the atlas.

rows.title: Who's laughing? Play, tickling and ultrasonic vocalizations in rats
rows.reason: Filed against another finding in the atlas (Panksepp 2011), which reads: "Rats produce 50-kHz ultrasonic chirps during play that are homologous to human laughter. These joyful sounds are most abundant during rough-and-tumble play and human-administered tickling." The authors still describe both play and tickling as positive for the rat, so the record does not find the opposite of a positive state; what failed is a within-play count correlation, which Panksepp 2011 does not state (it says calls are most abundant in play and tickling, and the atlas's other record of the same paper already records the missing correlation). It stays in the atlas.
